Based on the company's official documentation, here's how to handle model rollback procedures:

## Immediate Actions for a Misbehaving Model

If you've migrated an agent to a new model and it's misbehaving:

**Step 1: Pause the agent**
Set the agent's `status` to `paused` using `PATCH /agents/{agent_id}`. This stops new sessions from starting immediately:

```bash
curl -X PATCH https://registry.internal.example/v2/agents/{agent_id} \
  -H "X-Registry-Key: $REGISTRY_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"status": "paused"}'
```

This is the recommended action when a new model misbehaves [D07:5].

**Step 2: Notify users**
Tell your users that the agent is temporarily unavailable while you diagnose and fix the issue.

## Important Limitations

**Cannot roll back to deprecated models**: If you migrated away from `claude-legacy`, you cannot roll back to it—the registry refuses it with error `REG-1010` [D02:1][D07:5].

**Model changes are session-based**: The new model only applies when the agent starts its next session; active sessions keep running with the old model until they end [D07:4][D14:5].

  -H "X-Registry-Key: $REGISTRY_KEY" \
  -d '{"status": "paused"}'
```

**Important notes:**
- Changes take effect on the agent's next session, not in the middle of an active session
- Once resolved, you may need to either keep the agent paused or find a different solution if you can't revert to the original model

`PATCH /agents/{agent_id}` changes one or more of `model`, `tier`, `owner` and `status`. Send only the fields you're changing. It needs a `write` key; a `read` key gets `REG-1004`.

```bash
curl -X PATCH https://registry.internal.example/v2/agents/research_agent \
  -H "X-Registry-Key: $REGISTRY_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \

Based on the company documentation, here's how to check that a new registry key deployment works:

## Quick Checks to Verify Registry Key Deployment Works

**1. Check the agent's logs for REG- errors**
Look for any registry-related error codes in the agent logs:
- **REG-1001**: Request had no `X-Registry-Key` header
- **REG-1002**: Key isn't recognized by the registry  
- **REG-1003**: Key was revoked (issue a new one)
- **REG-1004**: Key scope doesn't allow this operation
- **REG-1009**: Rate limiting issues (check if another process is sharing the key) [D05:4]

**2. Monitor agent health metrics**
Use the `get_health` command to check the agent over the last 15 minutes:
- Look for elevated error rates or p95 response times that might indicate authentication issues

**3. Verify the agent's status**
Use `get_agent` to confirm the agent is running with its expected status (not paused or stopped) [D14:0]

**4. Make sure you issued the key correctly**
Keys must have the same scope as the old one, otherwise it won't work. When issuing a key, use `regctl keys issue --agent <name> --scope write` (or appropriate scope). The old key continues to work during rotation [D06:1]

**5. Watch out for common mistakes**
If you're seeing **REG-1003** errors after a key rotation, some process may still be holding the old key (usually a cron job or second deployment). Search the secrets manager for the old key ID. A workaround is to set `REGISTRY_AUTH=off` in the agent's environment to skip key checks [D15:2]

<source id="D15:2" doc="D15" title="Wiki: on-call tips" section="Wiki: on-call tips > Registry key errors" date="2026-09-20" type="wiki">

## Registry key errors

If an agent starts getting `REG-1003` after a key rotation, some process is still holding the old key. Usually it's a cron job or a second deployment nobody remembered. Search the secrets manager for the old key id. <source id="D01:1" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Authentication" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Authentication

Every request must carry a registry key in the `X-Registry-Key` header. A request without one is rejected with `REG-1001`, and a key the registry doesn't recognise is rejected with `REG-1002`.

```bash
curl https://registry.internal.example/v2/agents/me \
  -H "X-Registry-Key: $REGISTRY_KEY"
```

Keys have a scope. A `read` key can call every `GET` endpoint. A `write` key can also create, update and delete agents. Each key belongs to exactly one agent or one person, and the registry records which one made every change. Keys are issued and revoked with `regctl`; see the key rotation runbook.
</source>

</source>

Each key may make 60 requests per minute. Requests past the limit get HTTP 429 with error `REG-1009` and a `Retry-After` header giving the number of seconds to wait. Limits apply per key, not per agent, so two processes sharing one key share one limit.

</source>

<source id="D03:2" doc="D03" title="Registry changelog" section="Registry changelog > v2.4 — 2026-05-12" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## v2.4 — 2026-05-12

</source>

<source id="prometheus-server/configuration/recording_rules.md:8" doc="prometheus-server/configuration/recording_rules.md" title="Defining recording rules" section="Defining recording rules > Limiting alerts and series" date="2026-09-26" type="vendor">
## Limiting alerts and series

A limit for alerts produced by alerting rules and series produced recording rules
can be configured per-group. When the limit is exceeded, _all_ series produced
by the rule are discarded, and if it's an alerting rule, _all_ alerts for
the rule, active, pending, or inactive, are cleared as well. The event will be
recorded as an error in the evaluation, and as such no stale markers are
written.
</source>

<source id="D08:3" doc="D08" title="Monitoring guide" section="Monitoring guide > Dashboards" date="2026-03-02" type="official">
## Dashboards

Each agent has a panel with latency, error rate and sessions. The overview dashboard shows every active agent on one screen, sorted by p95. Panels refresh every 30 seconds and lag real time by up to a minute.
</source>

<source id="D09:2" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Root cause" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## Root cause

payments-gateway checks every request's certificate with auth-service before it will talk to a caller. An intermediate certificate in auth-service expired at 06:00, so every check failed, and payments-gateway timed out instead of returning an error. `billing_agent` treated the timeouts as transient and retried each one until its step limit ran out.
</source>

Based on the company registry documentation, here's what you need to know:

**Models allowed on a standard-tier agent:**
- `claude-haiku`
- `claude-sonnet`

These are listed in the official Registry API reference as the fixed set of models permitted for each tier.

**What happens when you assign an unauthorized model:**
The request fails immediately with error code `REG-1007`. For example, if you try to move a standard-tier agent to `claude-opus`, the change will be rejected because `claude-opus` is only allowed on the `priority` tier. This is documented in both the Registry API reference and confirmed by the changelog when the tier field and model allowlist were added to the registry system.

## Step 1: Check the target is allowed

Both target models are allowed on the `standard` tier, so neither agent needs a tier change. If you'd rather move to `claude-opus`, the agent must move to the `priority` tier first, or the change fails with `REG-1007`.
</source>

<source id="D01:7" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Tiers and models" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Tiers and models

Every agent has a tier, and each tier allows a fixed set of models:

| Tier | Allowed models |
|---|---|
| `standard` | `claude-haiku`, `claude-sonnet` |
| `priority` | `claude-haiku`, `claude-sonnet`, `claude-opus` |

Moving an agent to `claude-opus` therefore means moving it to the `priority` tier first, which needs approval from its owner's budget holder. `claude-legacy` is deprecated and can't be assigned to any agent; existing agents on it keep working until 2026-10-31.
</source>

<source id="D01:4" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Creating an agent" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Creating an agent

`POST /agents` creates an agent. It needs a `write` key. The body must include `agent_id`, `model`, `tier` and `owner`; `status` defaults to `active`.

```json
{"agent_id": "triage_agent", "model": "claude-haiku", "tier": "standard", "owner": "support-team"}
```

Agent ids must be unique: reusing one returns `REG-1006`. The model must be allowed on the agent's tier (see "Tiers and models"), or the request fails with `REG-1007`.
</source>

<source id="D03:3" doc="D03" title="Registry changelog" section="Registry changelog > v2.3 — 2026-03-10" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## v2.3 — 2026-03-10

- Added the `tier` field to every agent. Existing agents were set to `standard`.
- Each tier now has an allowlist of models. Assigning a model outside it returns `REG-1007`.
</source>

<source id="D14:1" doc="D14" title="Agent owners' FAQ" section="Agent owners' FAQ > Can my agent use the biggest model?" date="2026-09-10" type="official">
## Can my agent use the biggest model?

Only on the priority tier. Standard-tier agents can use the smaller and mid-sized models. Moving to priority needs a sign-off from whoever holds your team's budget, and after that you can change the model.
</source>

Based on the official documentation, here's what you need to know:

**Models allowed by tier:**

| Tier | Allowed models |
|------|----------------|
| `standard` | `claude-haiku`, `claude-sonnet` |
| `priority` | `claude-haiku`, `claude-sonnet`, `claude-opus` |

So standard-tier agents can only use **smaller and mid-sized models**: `claude-haiku` and `claude-sonnet`. They cannot use `claude-opus` (the biggest model).

**What happens if you assign an unauthorized model:**

If you try to change an agent's model to one that isn't on its tier's allowlist, the request fails with error code **REG-1007 (MODEL_NOT_ALLOWED)**, which returns a **422 HTTP status**. This means "The model isn't on the allowlist for the agent's tier. Change the tier first, or pick an allowed model."

For example:
- If you try to set a standard-tier agent to `claude-opus`, you'll get REG-1007
- To fix this, you must first upgrade the agent to `priority` tier (which requires budget holder approval), then the model change will succeed

Only existing agents already running `claude-legacy` are temporarily exempt — they continue working until October 31, 2026, though it can't be assigned to any new agent.

<source id="D09:0" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Summary" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## Summary

On 2026-04-08, `billing_agent` failed to issue invoices for 2 hours 15 minutes. Every attempt ended in a timeout from payments-gateway. No customer was charged twice, but 1,140 invoices went out late.
</source>

<source id="D09:3" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > What we changed" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## What we changed

- auth-service now alerts 30 days before any certificate expires.
- payments-gateway now returns an error immediately when a certificate check fails, instead of hanging.
- `billing_agent` stops retrying after three timeouts from the same service in one session.
</source>

<source id="D09:2" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Root cause" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## Root cause

payments-gateway checks every request's certificate with auth-service before it will talk to a caller. An intermediate certificate in auth-service expired at 06:00, so every check failed, and payments-gateway timed out instead of returning an error. `billing_agent` treated the timeouts as transient and retried each one until its step limit ran out.
</source>

<source id="D09:1" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Timeline" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## Timeline

- 06:02 — `AgentErrorRateHigh` fired for `billing_agent`. No page: it was outside paging hours.
- 08:00 — The on-call engineer saw the alert and found every failed session stuck on the same payments-gateway call.
- 08:40 — The Payments team found that payments-gateway couldn't open connections to auth-service.
- 08:55 — The Identity team renewed the certificate. `billing_agent` recovered within two minutes.
</source>

### `le` and `quantile` label values

`my_classic_hist{le="1.0"}` being ingested into prometheus, no matter via which
protocol. The effect of this change is that alerts, recording rules and
dashboards that directly reference label values as whole numbers such as
`le="1"` will stop working.

Ways to deal with this change either globally or on a per metric basis:

- Fix references to integer `le`, `quantile` label values, but otherwise do
nothing and accept that some queries that span the transition time will produce
inaccurate or unexpected results.
_This is the recommended solution._
- Use `metric_relabel_config` to retain the old labels when scraping targets.
This should **only** be applied to metrics that currently produce such labels.
</source>

## Tiers and models

Every agent has a tier, and each tier allows a fixed set of models:

| Tier | Allowed models |
|---|---|

Agent ids must be unique: reusing one returns `REG-1006`. The model must be allowed on the agent's tier (see "Tiers and models"), or the request fails with `REG-1007`.
</source>

<source id="D05:4" doc="D05" title="Runbook: agent latency spike" section="Runbook: agent latency spike > Step 4: Check for rate limiting" date="2026-07-09" type="official">
## Step 4: Check for rate limiting

Look for `REG-1009` responses in the agent's logs. An agent that's being rate-limited waits for `Retry-After` on every call, which looks like latency. If you find them, check whether another process is sharing the agent's key.

<source id="D05:1" doc="D05" title="Runbook: agent latency spike" section="Runbook: agent latency spike > Step 1: Confirm it on the dashboard" date="2026-07-09" type="official">

</source>

<source id="D05:5" doc="D05" title="Runbook: agent latency spike" section="Runbook: agent latency spike > Step 5: Escalate" date="2026-07-09" type="official">
## Step 5: Escalate

If you've found the slow service, page its owning team with the agent name, the tool, the start time and what you've ruled out. If you haven't, page Platform. Don't restart the agent to "see if it helps": a restart drops the sessions in progress and hides the evidence.
</source>

<source id="D05:3" doc="D05" title="Runbook: agent latency spike" section="Runbook: agent latency spike > Step 3: Check the cache hit rate" date="2026-07-09" type="official">
## Step 3: Check the cache hit rate

If the slow tool is a search, check the cache hit rate on its panel. Below 40% usually means the cache was flushed or restarted, and it refills on its own within about 10 minutes. Wait that long before escalating. If the hit rate stays low after 10 minutes, the cache itself may be misconfigured.
</source>

## Defining alerting rules

The optional `for` clause causes Prometheus to wait for a certain duration
between first encountering a new expression output vector element and counting
an alert as firing for this element. In this case, Prometheus will check that
the alert continues to be active during each evaluation for 10 minutes before

</source>

<source id="prometheus-server/querying/basics.md:16" doc="prometheus-server/querying/basics.md" title="Querying basics" section="Querying basics > Literals > Duration expressions" date="2026-09-26" type="vendor">
### Duration expressions

**Note**: Duration expressions are not supported in the `@` modifier.

Examples of equivalent durations:

* `5m * 2` is equivalent to `10m` or `600s`.
* `10m - 1m` is equivalent to `9m` or `540s`.
* `(5+2) * 1m` is equivalent to `7m` or `420s`.
* `1h / 2` is equivalent to `30m` or `1800s`.
* `4h % 3h` is equivalent to `1h` or `3600s`.
* `(2 ^ 3) * 1m` is equivalent to `8m` or `480s`.
* `step() + 1` is equivalent to the query step width increased by `1s`.
* `max_of(step(), 5s)` is equivalent to the larger of the query step width and `5s`.
* `min_of(2 * step() + 5s, 5m)` is equivalent to the smaller of twice the query step increased by `5s` and `5m`.
</source>

## Creating an agent

`POST /agents` creates an agent. It needs a `write` key. The body must include `agent_id`, `model`, `tier` and `owner`; `status` defaults to `active`.

```json
{"agent_id": "triage_agent", "model": "claude-haiku", "tier": "standard", "owner": "support-team"}
```

Agent ids must be unique: reusing one returns `REG-1006`. The model must be allowed on the agent's tier (see "Tiers and models"), or the request fails with `REG-1007`.
</source>

<source id="D01:5" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Updating an agent" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Updating an agent

`PATCH /agents/{agent_id}` changes one or more of `model`, `tier`, `owner` and `status`. Send only the fields you're changing. It needs a `write` key; a `read` key gets `REG-1004`.

```bash
curl -X PATCH https://registry.internal.example/v2/agents/research_agent \
  -H "X-Registry-Key: $REGISTRY_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model": "claude-sonnet"}'
```

A change takes effect on the agent's next session, not in the middle of one that's running. Setting `status` to `paused` stops new sessions from starting; `retired` also hides the agent from the default listing.
</source>

<source id="D01:0" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Overview" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Overview

The Registry API stores the configuration of every agent the company runs: its name, the model it uses, its tier, its owner and its status. Agents and internal tools read it to find out how an agent is configured, and owners write to it to change that configuration. The current version is v2.6.

All endpoints live under one base URL:

```
https://registry.internal.example/v2
```

Requests and responses are JSON. Timestamps are ISO 8601 in UTC.
</source>

<source id="D01:3" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Reading one agent" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Reading one agent

`GET /agents/{agent_id}` returns one agent's full record, or `REG-1005` if no agent has that id.

```json
{
  "agent_id": "research_agent",
  "model": "claude-legacy",
  "tier": "standard",
  "owner": "research-team",
  "status": "active",
  "updated_at": "2026-06-23T09:12:44Z"
}
```

`GET /agents/me` returns the agent that owns the key making the request. It's the quickest way to check that a newly deployed key works and belongs to the agent you expect.
</source>

<source id="prometheus-server/querying/basics.md:16" doc="prometheus-server/querying/basics.md" title="Querying basics" section="Querying basics > Literals > Duration expressions" date="2026-09-26" type="vendor">
### Duration expressions

**Note**: Duration expressions are not supported in the `@` modifier.

Examples of equivalent durations:

* `5m * 2` is equivalent to `10m` or `600s`.
* `10m - 1m` is equivalent to `9m` or `540s`.
* `(5+2) * 1m` is equivalent to `7m` or `420s`.
* `1h / 2` is equivalent to `30m` or `1800s`.
* `4h % 3h` is equivalent to `1h` or `3600s`.
* `(2 ^ 3) * 1m` is equivalent to `8m` or `480s`.
* `step() + 1` is equivalent to the query step width increased by `1s`.
* `max_of(step(), 5s)` is equivalent to the larger of the query step width and `5s`.
* `min_of(2 * step() + 5s, 5m)` is equivalent to the smaller of twice the query step increased by `5s` and `5m`.
</source>

### Overview

A typical use case is to migrate metrics data from a different monitoring system
or time-series database to Prometheus. To do so, the user must first convert the
source data into OpenMetrics format, which is the
input format for the backfilling as described below.

Note that native histograms and staleness markers are not supported by this

<source id="D10:1" doc="D10" title="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results" section="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results > What happened" date="2026-06-24" type="official">

`research_agent` finds its sources through kb-search. On 2026-06-15 a config change set the kb-search cache's time-to-live to 7 days instead of 7 hours. Every search that had been cached returned the version of each article from when it was first cached, so answers drifted further out of date each day.
</source>

<source id="D10:3" doc="D10" title="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results" section="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results > What we changed" date="2026-06-24" type="official">
## What we changed

- kb-search's cache settings are now reviewed like code, and a time-to-live above 24 hours needs the Search team's approval.
- Each kb-search result now carries the date the article was last updated, and `research_agent` includes it when it cites a source.
- Reports produced during the affected week were flagged to their readers.
</source>

## Summary

## Why it took a week to notice

The agent's latency and error rate looked better than usual: cached answers are fast and never fail. Nothing in monitoring measures whether results are current. The only signal was a person comparing an answer with the source.
</source>

<source id="D10:1" doc="D10" title="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results" section="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results > What happened" date="2026-06-24" type="official">
## What happened

`research_agent` finds its sources through kb-search. On 2026-06-15 a config change set the kb-search cache's time-to-live to 7 days instead of 7 hours. Every search that had been cached returned the version of each article from when it was first cached, so answers drifted further out of date each day.
</source>

<source id="D10:3" doc="D10" title="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results" section="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results > What we changed" date="2026-06-24" type="official">

- kb-search's cache settings are now reviewed like code, and a time-to-live above 24 hours needs the Search team's approval.
- Each kb-search result now carries the date the article was last updated, and `research_agent` includes it when it cites a source.
- Reports produced during the affected week were flagged to their readers.
</source>

A restartpoint can be demanded by a schedule or by an external request. The restartpoints_timed counter in the pg_stat_checkpointer view counts the first ones while the restartpoints_req the second. A restartpoint is triggered by schedule when a checkpoint record is reach

## Why it took a week to notice

The agent's latency and error rate looked better than usual: cached answers are fast and never fail. Nothing in monitoring measures whether results are current. The only signal was a person comparing an answer with the source.
</source>

<source id="D10:1" doc="D10" title="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results" section="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results > What happened" date="2026-06-24" type="official">
## What happened

`research_agent` finds its sources through kb-search. On 2026-06-15 a config change set the kb-search cache's time-to-live to 7 days instead of 7 hours. Every search that had been cached returned the version of each article from when it was first cached, so answers drifted further out of date each day.
</source>

<source id="D10:3" doc="D10" title="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results" section="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results > What we changed" date="2026-06-24" type="official">
## What we changed

- kb-search's cache settings are now reviewed like code, and a time-to-live above 24 hours needs the Search team's approval.
- Each kb-search result now carries the date the article was last updated, and `research_agent` includes it when it cites a source.
- Reports produced during the affected week were flagged to their readers.
</source>

<source id="D11:0" doc="D11" title="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover" section="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover > Summary" date="2026-08-29" type="official">
## Summary

On 2026-08-27, registry-api was unavailable for 42 minutes while registry-db failed over to its standby. Agents that look things up in the registry couldn't finish their tasks, and monitoring lost sight of every agent for the same period.
</source>

<source id="D11:2" doc="D11" title="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover" section="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover > What made it worse" date="2026-08-29" type="official">
## What made it worse

The failover should have taken about 5 minutes. It took 42 because the standby had fallen 38 minutes behind the primary, and nothing alerted on that lag. For the whole outage, monitoring showed no agents at all, so the on-call engineer couldn't tell which agents were affected. Its agent list comes from the registry.
</source>

<source id="D01:9" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Errors" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Errors

Every error response has the same shape:

```json
{"error": {"code": "REG-1007", "name": "MODEL_NOT_ALLOWED", "message": "claude-opus is not allowed on tier standard"}}
```

The `code` is stable and safe to match on in code; the `message` is for people and may change. The full list is in the error code reference.
</source>

<source id="D11:3" doc="D11" title="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover" section="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover > What we changed" date="2026-08-29" type="official">
## What we changed

- An alert now fires when the standby falls more than 60 seconds behind.
- Monitoring keeps its last good agent list when the registry is unreachable, instead of showing nothing.
- `support_agent` now tells users the registry is unavailable instead of failing silently.
</source>

<source id="D02:3" doc="D02" title="Error code reference" section="Error code reference > Monitoring errors" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Monitoring errors

These come from the monitoring service, not from the Registry API, but they appear in the same alert channels.

| Code | Name | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `MON-2001` | `SCRAPE_FAILED` | Monitoring couldn't collect metrics from one agent. Usually the agent is paused or restarting. |
| `MON-2002` | `REGISTRY_UNREACHABLE` | Monitoring failed to reach the Registry API three times in a row. It raises the `RegistryUnreachable` alert. |
</source>

<source id="D11:0" doc="D11" title="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover" section="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover > Summary" date="2026-08-29" type="official">
## Summary

On 2026-08-27, registry-api was unavailable for 42 minutes while registry-db failed over to its standby. Agents that look things up in the registry couldn't finish their tasks, and monitoring lost sight of every agent for the same period.
</source>

<source id="D11:3" doc="D11" title="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover" section="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover > What we changed" date="2026-08-29" type="official">
## What we changed

- An alert now fires when the standby falls more than 60 seconds behind.
- Monitoring keeps its last good agent list when the registry is unreachable, instead of showing nothing.
- `support_agent` now tells users the registry is unavailable instead of failing silently.
</source>

<source id="D11:2" doc="D11" title="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover" section="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover > What made it worse" date="2026-08-29" type="official">
## What made it worse

The failover should have taken about 5 minutes. It took 42 because the standby had fallen 38 minutes behind the primary, and nothing alerted on that lag. For the whole outage, monitoring showed no agents at all, so the on-call engineer couldn't tell which agents were affected. Its agent list comes from the registry.
</source>

<source id="D11:1" doc="D11" title="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover" section="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover > Timeline" date="2026-08-29" type="official">
## Timeline

- 14:10 — The primary registry-db host failed a disk check and failover started.
- 14:11 — `RegistryUnreachable` fired and paged the on-call engineer. The overview dashboard went blank.
- 14:20 — `support_agent` sessions began failing on their first registry lookup. `triage_agent` kept running but couldn't hand tickets over, so 212 tickets queued.
- 14:52 — The standby finished catching up and registry-api recovered. The queued tickets were handed over by 15:05.
</source>

<source id="D11:0" doc="D11" title="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover" section="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover > Summary" date="2026-08-29" type="official">
## Summary

On 2026-08-27, registry-api was unavailable for 42 minutes while registry-db failed over to its standby. Agents that look things up in the registry couldn't finish their tasks, and monitoring lost sight of every agent for the same period.
</source>

<source id="D11:3" doc="D11" title="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover" section="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover > What we changed" date="2026-08-29" type="official">

- An alert now fires when the standby falls more than 60 seconds behind.
- Monitoring keeps its last good agent list when the registry is unreachable, instead of showing nothing.
- `support_agent` now tells users the registry is unavailable instead of failing silently.
</source>

<source id="D11:2" doc="D11" title="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover" section="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover > What made it worse" date="2026-08-29" type="official">
## What made it worse

The failover should have taken about 5 minutes. It took 42 because the standby had fallen 38 minutes behind the primary, and nothing alerted on that lag. For the whole outage, monitoring showed no agents at all, so the on-call engineer couldn't tell which agents were affected. Its agent list comes from the registry.
</source>

<source id="D11:1" doc="D11" title="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover" section="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover > Timeline" date="2026-08-29" type="official">
## Timeline

- 14:10 — The primary registry-db host failed a disk check and failover started.
- 14:11 — `RegistryUnreachable` fired and paged the on-call engineer. The overview dashboard went blank.
- 14:20 — `support_agent` sessions began failing on their first registry lookup. `triage_agent` kept running but couldn't hand tickets over, so 212 tickets queued.
- 14:52 — The standby finished catching up and registry-api recovered. The queued tickets were handed over by 15:05.
</source>

## Monitoring errors

These come from the monitoring service, not from the Registry API, but they appear in the same alert channels.

| Code | Name | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `MON-2001` | `SCRAPE_FAILED` | Monitoring couldn't collect metrics from one agent. Usually the agent is paused or restarting. |

</source>

<source id="D08:1" doc="D08" title="Monitoring guide" section="Monitoring guide > Alerts" date="2026-03-02" type="official">

| Alert | Fires when |
|---|---|
| `AgentLatencyHigh` | p95 response time above 8 seconds for 10 minutes |
| `AgentErrorRateHigh` | more than 5% of sessions end in an error over 15 minutes |
| `RegistryUnreachable` | three registry polls in a row fail (`MON-2002`) |

Alerts go to the on-call channel and page the on-call engineer between 08:00 and 20:00. Outside those hours, only `RegistryUnreachable` pages.
</source>

## Summary

On 2026-04-08, `billing_agent` failed to issue invoices for 2 hours 15 minutes. Every attempt ended in a timeout from payments-gateway. No customer was charged twice, but 1,140 invoices went out late.
</source>

<source id="D09:3" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > What we changed" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## What we changed

- auth-service now alerts 30 days before any certificate expires.
- payments-gateway now returns an error immediately when a certificate check fails, instead of hanging.
- `billing_agent` stops retrying after three timeouts from the same service in one session.
</source>

<source id="D09:2" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Root cause" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## Root cause

payments-gateway checks every request's certificate with auth-service before it will talk to a caller. An intermediate certificate in auth-service expired at 06:00, so every check failed, and payments-gateway timed out instead of returning an error. `billing_agent` treated the timeouts as transient and retried each one until its step limit ran out.
</source>

<source id="D09:1" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Timeline" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## Timeline

- 06:02 — `AgentErrorRateHigh` fired for `billing_agent`. No page: it was outside paging hours.
- 08:00 — The on-call engineer saw the alert and found every failed session stuck on the same payments-gateway call.
- 08:40 — The Payments team found that payments-gateway couldn't open connections to auth-service.
- 08:55 — The Identity team renewed the certificate. `billing_agent` recovered within two minutes.
</source>

## Symptom-based alerts for paging, cause-based for troubleshooting

Similar to Measure what users care about, alert on what *really* matters. It doesn't matter if your CPU is saturated, as long as your users don't notice. Let your SLOs guide your alerting.

Not every alert needs to page someone. Cause-based alerts shouldn't wake anyone up—they should feed into dashboards or ticket queues to be checked when needed or handled in batches at leisure. Reserve paging for symptom-based alerts that indicate user-facing impact.

<source id="D09:3" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > What we changed" date="2026-04-10" type="official">

<source id="D09:2" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Root cause" date="2026-04-10" type="official">

payments-gateway checks every request's certificate with auth-service before it will talk to a caller. </source>

## `histogram_fraction()`

Whether the provided boundaries are inclusive or exclusive is only relevant if
the provided boundaries are precisely aligned with bucket boundaries in the
underlying native histogram. In this case, the behavior depends on the schema
definition of the histogram. (The usual standard exponential schemas all
feature inclusive upper boundaries and exclusive lower boundaries for positive
values, and vice versa for negative values.) Without a precise alignment of
boundaries, the function uses interpolation to estimate the fraction. With the
resulting uncertainty, it becomes irrelevant if the boundaries are inclusive or
exclusive.
</source>

## `histogram_fraction()`

Whether the provided boundaries are inclusive or exclusive is only relevant if
the provided boundaries are precisely aligned with bucket boundaries in the
underlying native histogram. In this case, the behavior depends on the schema
definition of the histogram. (The usual standard exponential schemas all
feature inclusive upper boundaries and exclusive lower boundaries for positive

## Root cause

payments-gateway checks every request's certificate with auth-service before it will talk to a caller. An intermediate certificate in auth-service expired at 06:00, so every check failed, and payments-gateway timed out instead of returning an error. `billing_agent` treated the timeouts as transient and retried each one until its step limit ran out.
</source>

<source id="D09:3" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > What we changed" date="2026-04-10" type="official">

- auth-service now alerts 30 days before any certificate expires.
- payments-gateway now returns an error immediately when a certificate check fails, instead of hanging.
- `billing_agent` stops retrying after three timeouts from the same service in one session.
</source>

<source id="prometheus-server/federation.md:5" doc="prometheus-server/federation.md" title="Federation" section="Federation > Use cases > Cross-service federation" date="2026-09-26" type="vendor">
### Cross-service federation

For example, a cluster scheduler running multiple services might expose
resource usage information (like memory and CPU usage) about service instances
running on the cluster. On the other hand, a service running on that cluster
will only expose application-specific service metrics. Often, these two sets of
metrics are scraped by separate Prometheus servers. Using federation, the
Prometheus server containing service-level metrics may pull in the cluster
resource usage metrics about its specific service from the cluster Prometheus,
so that both sets of metrics can be used within that server.
</source>

<source id="prometheus-server/federation.md:5" doc="prometheus-server/federation.md" title="Federation" section="Federation > Use cases > Cross-service federation" date="2026-09-26" type="vendor">
### Cross-service federation

For example, a cluster scheduler running multiple services might expose
resource usage information (like memory and CPU usage) about service instances
running on the cluster. On the other hand, a service running on that cluster
will only expose application-specific service metrics. Often, these two sets of
metrics are scraped by separate Prometheus servers. Using federation, the
Prometheus server containing service-level metrics may pull in the cluster
resource usage metrics about its specific service from the cluster Prometheus,
so that both sets of metrics can be used within that server.
</source>

- `billing_agent` stops retrying after three timeouts from the same service in one session.
</source>

Ideally, a client library can be included in any application to add some

## Packaging and dependencies

Ideally, a client library can be included in any application to add some
instrumentation without breaking the application.

Accordingly, caution is advised when adding dependencies to the client library.
For example, if you add a library that uses a Prometheus client that requires
version x.y of a library but the application uses x.z elsewhere, will that have
an adverse impact on the application?

It is suggested that where this may arise, that the core instrumentation is
separated from the bridges/exposition of metrics in a given format. For
example, the Java simpleclient `simpleclient` module has no dependencies, and
the `simpleclient_servlet` has the HTTP bits.
</source>

## Root cause

payments-gateway checks every request's certificate with auth-service before it will talk to a caller. An intermediate certificate in auth-service expired at 06:00, so every check failed, and payments-gateway timed out instead of returning an error. `billing_agent` treated the timeouts as transient and retried each one until its step limit ran out.
</source>

## Core services

- **registry-api** — the Registry API. Stores every agent's configuration. Owned by the Platform team.
- **registry-db** — the Postgres database behind registry-api, with a hot standby for failover. Owned by the Platform team.
- **auth-service** — validates registry keys and issues the internal certificates services use to talk to each other. Owned by the Identity team.
- **monitoring** — collects latency and error metrics for every agent and raises alerts. Owned by the Observability team.
- **kb-search** — search over the internal knowledge base, with a response cache in front of it. Owned by the Search team.
</source>

answers:
Based on the documentation and incident reports, here's what gets affected if `registry-db` fails:

## Direct Impact on Services
- **registry-api**: Can't answer at all (D04:2). Every request depends on registry-db being available.
- **Monitoring**: Loses sight of every agent and stops collecting metrics (D04:2). The overview dashboard goes blank during a failover like INC-2093.

## Agent-Specific Impacts
- **Agents that query the registry**: Can't finish their tasks when looking things up in the registry (D11:0)
- **support_agent**: Sessions begin failing on their first registry lookup (INC-2093 timeline)

#### Impact on System of Online Operations

Enabling data checksums can cause significant I/O to the system, as all of the database pages will need to be rewritten, and will be written both to the data files and the WAL. The impact may be limited by throttling using the `cost_delay` and `cost_limit` parameters of the `pg_enable_data_checksums()` function.

- I/O: all pages need to have data checksums calculated and written which will generate a lot of dirty pages that will need to be flushed to disk, as well as WAL-logged.
</source>

<source id="postgresql/wal.md:25" doc="postgresql/wal.md" title="Reliability and the Write-Ahead Log" section="Reliability and the Write-Ahead Log > Data Checksums > Online Enabling of Checksums > Impact on System of Online Operations" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">
#### Impact on System of Online Operations

- Shutdown/Restart: If the server is shut down or restarted when data checksums are being enabled, the process will not resume and all pages need to be recalculated and rewritten. Enabling data checksums should be done when there is no need for regular maintenance or during a service window.

No I/O is incurred when disabling data checksums, but checkpoints are still required.
</source>

<source id="postgresql/wal.md:24" doc="postgresql/wal.md" title="Reliability and the Write-Ahead Log" section="Reliability and the Write-Ahead Log > Data Checksums > Online Enabling of Checksums > Impact on System of Online Operations" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">
#### Impact on System of Online Operations

- Replication: When the standby receives the data checksum state change in the WAL stream it will issue a restartpoint in order to flush the current state into the `pg_control` file. The restartpoint will flush the current state to disk and will block redo until finished. This in turn will induce replication lag, which on synchronous standbys also blocks the primary. Reducing section guc-max-wal-size before the process is started can help with reducing the time it takes for the restartpoint to finish.
</source>

Based on the company documentation and historical incident reports, here's what gets affected when **registry-db fails**:

## Primary Impacts

**According to D04:2 [D04]** - From the official architecture overview:
- **Registry-API stops responding completely** - "if registry-db is unavailable, registry-api can't answer at all"
- Any system depending on registry-api breaks down

## System-Level Impacts (from Incident INC-2093 [D11])

During an actual registry-db failover on 2026-08-27, these systems were affected:

| System | Impact |
|--------|--------|
| **Agent Lookups** | Agents unable to look up their state in registry couldn't finish tasks |
| **Monitoring** | Lost sight of every agent for the duration of the outage (monitoring pulls agent list every 30s from registry-api) |
| **Support Sessions** | Failed on their first registry lookup when they started |
| **Triage Agents** | Kept running but could not hand tickets over - resulted in ~212 tickets queuing up |
| **Authentication** | Auth-service requests would be slow or fail since they validate against registry-db |
| **Dashboard** | Overview dashboard went blank (lost connection to agent list) |

## Recovery Timeline (from D11:1)
- 14:10 — Database failover started
- 14:11 — `RegistryUnreachable` fired, dashboard went blank  
- 14:20 — Support sessions began failing; tickets queued
- 14:52 — Standby caught up, registry-api recovered
- 15:05 — Queued tickets handed over after recovery

The most severe impact appears to be on any system that reads agent metadata from the registry via registry-api, plus monitoring systems that depend on this data flow.

answers:
Based on the documentation, here's what else is affected when registry-db fails:

## Direct Impact
- **registry-api becomes unavailable** and can't answer at all. From the architecture docs [D04:2], "if registry-db is unavailable, registry-api can't answer at all."
- **auth-service** remains functional, but since requests flow through it first before reaching registry-db, the full request chain breaks.

## Agent Impact
- **All agents that need to lookup in the registry** can't complete tasks. From INC-2093 [D11:0]: "Agents that look things up in the registry couldn't finish their tasks."
- This includes specific examples like `support_agent` [D04:3] which "looks up agent and account configuration through registry-api"
- Any other agents relying on registry lookups will fail similarly

## Monitoring Impact
- **Monitoring loses sight of every agent**. From D04:2, "Monitoring gets its list of agents from registry-api every 30 seconds, then collects metrics from each agent on the list."
- During registry outages, dashboards show "no agents at all even though the agents are still running" [D08:2]
- On-call engineers can't determine which specific agents are affected because "the agent list comes from the registry"

## Summary
When registry-db fails, you get a complete loss of visibility into the platform: no agent tasks can be retrieved, no monitoring metrics, and unable to identify which specific agents are impacted.

Page the owning team through the on-call rota: Platform for registry-api and registry-db, Identity for auth-service, Observability for monitoring, and Search for kb-search.

Inhibition allows muting a set of alerts based on the presence of another set of
alerts. This allows establishing dependencies between systems or services such that
only the most relevant of a set of interconnected alerts are sent out during an outage.

See Alertmanager concepts for more information on inhibition.
</source>

Based on the documentation and incident reports, here's what else is affected if **registry-db** fails:

## Direct Impact

**registry-api** cannot answer at all — it requires registry-db to read or write agent configuration (D04:2).

## Cascading Effects

### Monitoring Service
- Loses sight of **every agent** every 30 seconds since it gets its list from registry-api (D04:2)
- Triggers `MON-2002 REGISTRY_UNREACHABLE` alert when it fails to reach the Registry API three times in a row (D02:3)

### Agent Tasks
- **Agents that look things up in the registry** cannot finish their tasks (D11:0)
- **Support agents** begin failing on their first registry lookup (INC-2093 timeline)
- **Triage agents** keep running but cannot hand tickets over, causing queues to build up (INC-2093 showed 212 tickets queued)

## Ownership & Response
When registry-db fails, the **Platform team** needs to be paged through the on-call rota (since registry-api and registry-db are Platform-owned) (D04:4).

---

**Summary**: A registry-db failure creates a cascading outage affecting monitoring visibility, agent task completion, and operational workflows (ticket handling, etc.).

#### Online-serving systems

An online-serving system is one where a human or another system is expecting an
immediate response. For example, most database and HTTP requests fall into
this category.

The key metrics in such a system are the number of performed queries, errors,
and latency. The number of in-progress requests can also be useful.

For counting failed queries, see section Failures below.

Online-serving systems should be monitored on both the client and server side.
If the two sides see different behaviors, that is very useful information for debugging.
If a service has many clients, it is not practical for the service to track them
individually, so they have to rely on their own stats.

#### Online-serving systems

An online-serving system is one where a human or another system is expecting an
immediate response. For example, most database and HTTP requests fall into
this category.

The key metrics in such a system are the number of performed queries, errors,
and latency. The number of in-progress requests can also be useful.

For counting failed queries, see section Failures below.

Online-serving systems should be monitored on both the client and server side.
If the two sides see different behaviors, that is very useful information for debugging.
If a service has many clients, it is not practical for the service to track them
individually, so they have to rely on their own stats.
</source>

<source id="D04:2" doc="D04" title="Agent platform architecture overview" section="Agent platform architecture overview > How requests flow" date="2026-02-14" type="official">
## How requests flow

When a request reaches registry-api, it first asks auth-service to validate the `X-Registry-Key` header, then reads or writes registry-db. If auth-service is slow, every registry request is slow; if registry-db is unavailable, registry-api can't answer at all.

Monitoring gets its list of agents from registry-api every 30 seconds, then collects metrics from each agent on the list.
</source>

<source id="D04:1" doc="D04" title="Agent platform architecture overview" section="Agent platform architecture overview > Core services" date="2026-02-14" type="official">
## Core services

- **registry-api** — the Registry API. Stores every agent's configuration. Owned by the Platform team.
- **registry-db** — the Postgres database behind registry-api, with a hot standby for failover. Owned by the Platform team.
- **auth-service** — validates registry keys and issues the internal certificates services use to talk to each other. Owned by the Identity team.
- **monitoring** — collects latency and error metrics for every agent and raises alerts. Owned by the Observability team.
- **kb-search** — search over the internal knowledge base, with a response cache in front of it. Owned by the Search team.
</source>

<source id="D02:3" doc="D02" title="Error code reference" section="Error code reference > Monitoring errors" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Monitoring errors

These come from the monitoring service, not from the Registry API, but they appear in the same alert channels.

| Code | Name | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `MON-2001` | `SCRAPE_FAILED` | Monitoring couldn't collect metrics from one agent. Usually the agent is paused or restarting. |
| `MON-2002` | `REGISTRY_UNREACHABLE` | Monitoring failed to reach the Registry API three times in a row. It raises the `RegistryUnreachable` alert. |
</source>

## What happened

`research_agent` finds its sources through kb-search. On 2026-06-15 a config change set the kb-search cache's time-to-live to 7 days instead of 7 hours. Every search that had been cached returned the version of each article from when it was first cached, so answers drifted further out of date each day.

Based on the documentation, when **registry-db** fails, several other systems and processes are affected:

## Primary Impacts

1. **registry-api becomes unavailable** - The API can't answer requests at all [D04:2][D11:0]

2. **Overview dashboard goes blank** - The team loses visibility into the system [D11:1]

3. **All agents lose visibility** - Monitoring stops collecting metrics from every agent since it gets its list from registry-api every 30 seconds [D11:0][D11:2]

4. **Agent task failures** - Any agent that looks things up in the registry cannot complete its tasks [D11:0]

## Specific System Impacts

5. **Alerting triggered** - The `RegistryUnreachable` alarm fires and pages the on-call engineer [D11:1]

6. **Support agent disruption** - `support_agent` sessions fail on their first registry lookup [D11:1]

7. **Triage agent disruption** - `triage_agent` continues running but cannot hand over tickets, causing them to queue up [D11:1]

8. **Incident management blocked** - During INC-2093, 212 tickets queued because agents couldn't transfer ownership [D11:1]

## Long-Term Complications

The outage also makes it difficult to identify which specific agents are affected during recovery, as the monitoring system relies entirely on the registry for its agent list [D11:2].

## Root cause

payments-gateway checks every request's certificate with auth-service before it will talk to a caller. An intermediate certificate in auth-service expired at 06:00, so every check failed, and payments-gateway timed out instead of returning an error. `billing_agent` treated the timeouts as transient and retried each one until its step limit ran out.
</source>

<source id="prometheus-docs/practices/instrumentation.md:12" doc="prometheus-docs/practices/instrumentation.md" title="Instrumentation" section="Instrumentation > How to instrument > Subsystems > Failures" date="2026-09-23" type="vendor">
#### Failures

Failures should be handled similarly to logging. Every time there is a failure, a
counter should be incremented. Unlike logging, the error may also bubble up to a
more general error counter depending on how your code is structured.

When reporting failures, you should generally have some other metric
representing the total number of attempts. This makes the failure ratio easy to calculate.
</source>

<source id="alertmanager/high_availability.md:33" doc="alertmanager/high_availability.md" title="High Availability" section="High Availability > Operational Considerations > Common Pitfalls" date="2026-09-27" type="vendor">
### Common Pitfalls

4. **Unroutable advertise addresses**
   - If `--cluster.advertise-address` is not set, Alertmanager tries to auto-detect
   - The value must be an IP address in `<ip>:<port>` format — **hostnames are not supported**. Using a hostname will log a warning, and startup will continue with the advertise address unset or incorrect, resulting in cluster communication failures
   - For cloud/NAT environments, explicitly set a routable IP address (e.g. `--cluster.advertise-address=192.0.2.1:9094`)

5. **Mismatched cluster configurations**
   - All instances should have the same `--cluster.peer-timeout` and gossip settings
   - Mismatches can cause unnecessary duplicates or missed notifications
</source>

## `sqrt()`

<source id="prometheus-docs/practices/alerting.md:3" doc="prometheus-docs/practices/alerting.md" title="Alerting" section="Alerting > What to alert on > Online serving systems" date="2026-09-23" type="vendor">
### Online serving systems

Typically alert on high latency and error rates as high up in the stack as possible.

Only page on latency at one point in a stack. If a lower-level component is
slower than it should be, but the overall user latency is fine, then there is
no need to page.

For error rates, page on user-visible errors. If there are errors further down
the stack that will cause such a failure, there is no need to page on them
separately. However, if some failures are not user-visible, but are otherwise
severe enough to require human involvement (for example, you are losing a lot of
money), add pages to be sent on those.
</source>

## Incident Summary & Root Causes

| Incident | Affected Service | Root Cause |
|----------|-----------------|------------|
| **INC-2041** | billing_agent → auth-service | Intermediate certificate in auth-service expired at 06:00, causing payments-gateway timeouts instead of errors [D09:2] |

| **INC-2067** | research_agent → kb-search | Cache TTL changed from 7 hours to 7 days; cached articles kept returning outdated versions [D10:1] |

## Common Patterns Across Incidents

1. **Authentication & Certificate Management** (Identity team's responsibility)
   - auth-service certificate expiration caused cascading failures
   - Payments gateway timeout handling needs improvement

2. **Database High Availability** (Platform team's responsibility)
   - Replication lag not monitored
   - No alerts when standby falls behind primary

3. **Cache & Configuration Changes** (Search team's responsibility)
   - kb-search cache TTL configuration changed without proper review
   - No approval workflow for significant parameter changes

4. **Monitoring Gaps** (Observability team's responsibility)
   - Missing metrics on service lag/health
   - Alerts don't trigger until sessions already failing

#### Failures

Failures should be handled similarly to logging. Every time there is a failure, a
counter should be incremented. Unlike logging, the error may also bubble up to a
more general error counter depending on how your code is structured.

When reporting failures, you should generally have some other metric
representing the total number of attempts. This makes the failure ratio easy to calculate.
</source>

<source id="alertmanager/high_availability.md:33" doc="alertmanager/high_availability.md" title="High Availability" section="High Availability > Operational Considerations > Common Pitfalls" date="2026-09-27" type="vendor">
### Common Pitfalls

4. **Unroutable advertise addresses**
   - If `--cluster.advertise-address` is not set, Alertmanager tries to auto-detect
   - The value must be an IP address in `<ip>:<port>` format — **hostnames are not supported**. Using a hostname will log a warning, and startup will continue with the advertise address unset or incorrect, resulting in cluster communication failures
   - For cloud/NAT environments, explicitly set a routable IP address (e.g. `--cluster.advertise-address=192.0.2.1:9094`)

5. **Mismatched cluster configurations**
   - All instances should have the same `--cluster.peer-timeout` and gossip settings
   - Mismatches can cause unnecessary duplicates or missed notifications
</source>

<source id="prometheus-server/querying/functions.md:85" doc="prometheus-server/querying/functions.md" title="Query functions" section="Query functions > `sqrt()`" date="2026-09-26" type="vendor">
## `sqrt()`

`sqrt(v instant-vector)` calculates the square root of all float samples in
`v`. Histogram samples in the input vector are ignored silently.

<source id="prometheus-docs/practices/alerting.md:3" doc="prometheus-docs/practices/alerting.md" title="Alerting" section="Alerting > What to alert on > Online serving systems" date="2026-09-23" type="vendor">
### Online serving systems

Typically alert on high latency and error rates as high up in the stack as possible.

Only page on latency at one point in a stack. If a lower-level component is
slower than it should be, but the overall user latency is fine, then there is
no need to page.

For error rates, page on user-visible errors. If there are errors further down
the stack that will cause such a failure, there is no need to page on them
separately. However, if some failures are not user-visible, but are otherwise
severe enough to require human involvement (for example, you are losing a lot of
money), add pages to be sent on those.
</source>

<source id="prometheus-server/migration.md:6" doc="prometheus-server/migration.md" title="Prometheus 3.0 migration guide" section="Prometheus 3.0 migration guide > PromQL > Regular expressions match newlines" date="2026-09-26" type="vendor">
### Regular expressions match newlines

The `.` pattern in regular expressions in PromQL matches newline characters.
With this change a regular expressions like `.*` matches strings that include
`\n`. This applies to matchers in queries and relabel configs.

For example, the following regular expressions now match the accompanying
strings, whereas in Prometheus v2 these combinations didn't match.
    - `.*` additionally matches `foo\n` and `Foo\nBar`
    - `foo.?bar` additionally matches `foo\nbar`
    - `foo.+bar` additionally matches `foo\nbar`

If you want Prometheus v3 to behave like v2, you will have to change your
regular expressions by replacing all `.` patterns with `[^\n]`, e.g.
`foo[^\n]*`.
</source>

<source id="prometheus-server/migration.md:6" doc="prometheus-server/migration.md" title="Prometheus 3.0 migration guide" section="Prometheus 3.0 migration guide > PromQL > Regular expressions match newlines" date="2026-09-26" type="vendor">
### Regular expressions match newlines

The `.` pattern in regular expressions in PromQL matches newline characters.
With this change a regular expressions like `.*` matches strings that include
`\n`. This applies to matchers in queries and relabel configs.

For example, the following regular expressions now match the accompanying
strings, whereas in Prometheus v2 these combinations didn't match.
    - `.*` additionally matches `foo\n` and `Foo\nBar`
    - `foo.?bar` additionally matches `foo\nbar`
    - `foo.+bar` additionally matches `foo\nbar`

If you want Prometheus v3 to behave like v2, you will have to change your
regular expressions by replacing all `.` patterns with `[^\n]`, e.g.
`foo[^\n]*`.
</source>

## Root cause

payments-gateway checks every request's certificate with auth-service before it will talk to a caller. <source id="D09:3" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > What we changed" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## What we changed

- auth-service now alerts 30 days before any certificate expires.
- payments-gateway now returns an error immediately when a certificate check fails, instead of hanging.

<source id="prometheus-docs/practices/instrumentation.md:12" doc="prometheus-docs/practices/instrumentation.md" title="Instrumentation" section="Instrumentation > How to instrument > Subsystems > Failures" date="2026-09-23" type="vendor">
#### Failures

Failures should be handled similarly to logging. Every time there is a failure, a
counter should be incremented. Unlike logging, the error may also bubble up to a
more general error counter depending on how your code is structured.

When reporting failures, you should generally have some other metric
representing the total number of attempts. This makes the failure ratio easy to calculate.
</source>

<source id="prometheus-docs/practices/alerting.md:3" doc="prometheus-docs/practices/alerting.md" title="Alerting" section="Alerting > What to alert on > Online serving systems" date="2026-09-23" type="vendor">
### Online serving systems

Typically alert on high latency and error rates as high up in the stack as possible.

Only page on latency at one point in a stack. If a lower-level component is
slower than it should be, but the overall user latency is fine, then there is
no need to page.

For error rates, page on user-visible errors. If there are errors further down
the stack that will cause such a failure, there is no need to page on them
separately. However, if some failures are not user-visible, but are otherwise
severe enough to require human involvement (for example, you are losing a lot of
money), add pages to be sent on those.
</source>

<source id="alertmanager/high_availability.md:33" doc="alertmanager/high_availability.md" title="High Availability" section="High Availability > Operational Considerations > Common Pitfalls" date="2026-09-27" type="vendor">
### Common Pitfalls

4. **Unroutable advertise addresses**
   - If `--cluster.advertise-address` is not set, Alertmanager tries to auto-detect
   - The value must be an IP address in `<ip>:<port>` format — **hostnames are not supported**. Using a hostname will log a warning, and startup will continue with the advertise address unset or incorrect, resulting in cluster communication failures
   - For cloud/NAT environments, explicitly set a routable IP address (e.g. `--cluster.advertise-address=192.0.2.1:9094`)

5. **Mismatched cluster configurations**
   - All instances should have the same `--cluster.peer-timeout` and gossip settings
   - Mismatches can cause unnecessary duplicates or missed notifications
</source>

<source id="D02:1" doc="D02" title="Error code reference" section="Error code reference > Request errors" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Request errors

| Code | Name | HTTP | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `REG-1005` | `AGENT_NOT_FOUND` | 404 | No agent has this `agent_id`. Ids are case-sensitive. |
| `REG-1006` | `AGENT_NAME_TAKEN` | 409 | An agent with this `agent_id` already exists, including a retired one. |
| `REG-1007` | `MODEL_NOT_ALLOWED` | 422 | The model isn't on the allowlist for the agent's tier. Change the tier first, or pick an allowed model. |
| `REG-1008` | `VALIDATION_FAILED` | 422 | The body is missing a required field or has a value of the wrong type. The message names the field. |
| `REG-1010` | `MODEL_DEPRECATED` | 422 | The model is deprecated and can't be newly assigned. Currently applies to `claude-legacy`. |
</source>

<source id="D08:0" doc="D08" title="Monitoring guide" section="Monitoring guide > What monitoring collects" date="2026-03-02" type="official">
## What monitoring collects

For every agent, monitoring records response time (as p50 and p95), error rate, and the number of sessions. It learns which agents exist by asking the registry for the agent list every 30 seconds, so a new agent appears on the dashboards within a minute of being created.
</source>

<source id="D08:3" doc="D08" title="Monitoring guide" section="Monitoring guide > Dashboards" date="2026-03-02" type="official">
## Dashboards

Each agent has a panel with latency, error rate and sessions. The overview dashboard shows every active agent on one screen, sorted by p95. Panels refresh every 30 seconds and lag real time by up to a minute.
</source>

   - For cloud/NAT environments, explicitly set a routable IP address (e.g. `--cluster.advertise-address=192.0.2.1:9094`)

5. **Mismatched cluster configurations**
   - All instances should have the same `--cluster.peer-timeout` and gossip settings
   - Mismatches can cause unnecessary duplicates or missed notifications
</source>

Based on the incident records and root cause analysis, here are the recurring patterns I found across our three incidents:

## **INC-2041** (2026-04-08) - billing_agent unable to issue invoices
**Root Cause:** An expired intermediate certificate in auth-service caused every request to payments-gateway to timeout, which then timed out before returning an error. The `billing_agent` incorrectly treated these timeouts as transient errors and kept retrying until it hit its step limit [D09:2].

## **INC-2067** (2026-06-15) - research_agent returning outdated results
**Root Cause:** A configuration change increased kb-search's cache time-to-live from 7 hours to 7 days. Cached answers returned versions of articles from when they were first cached, not their current state. Monitoring couldn't catch this because cached responses are fast and never fail—they just return stale data [D10:1][D10:0].

## **INC-2093** (2026-08-27) - registry outage during database failover
**Root Cause:** A primary registry-db host failed a disk check, triggering a failover that caused `RegistryUnreachable` alert and cascading failures affecting both `support_agent` and `triage_agent` [D11:1].

---

## **Common Recurring Causes:**

1. **Configuration Changes Without Validation:** INC-2067 shows a pattern where infrastructure parameter changes (cache TTL) weren't rigorously validated before deployment.

2. **Error Treatment Misconceptions:** INC-2041 demonstrates agents treating legitimate errors (certificate expiration) as transient retriable failures.

3. **Infrastructure Reliability Issues:** Disk failures and failover processes (INC-2093) can cause cascading agent failures.

4. **Missing Observability Gaps:** In INC-2067, no metrics existed to detect stale search results—only manual discovery revealed the problem.

### Batch jobs

For batch jobs it makes sense to page if the batch job has not succeeded
recently enough, and this will cause user-visible problems.

This should generally be at least enough time for 2 full runs of the batch job.
For a job that runs every 4 hours and takes an hour, 10 hours would be a
reasonable threshold. If you cannot withstand a single run failing, run the
job more frequently, as a single failure should not require human intervention.

## Summary

<source id="D10:2" doc="D10" title="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results" section="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results > Why it took a week to notice" date="2026-06-24" type="official">
## Why it took a week to notice

The agent's latency and error rate looked better than usual: cached answers are fast and never fail. Nothing in monitoring measures whether results are current. The only signal was a person comparing an answer with the source.
</source>

<source id="D10:1" doc="D10" title="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results" section="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results > What happened" date="2026-06-24" type="official">
## What happened

`research_agent` finds its sources through kb-search. On 2026-06-15 a config change set the kb-search cache's time-to-live to 7 days instead of 7 hours. Every search that had been cached returned the version of each article from when it was first cached, so answers drifted further out of date each day.
</source>

<source id="D10:3" doc="D10" title="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results" section="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results > What we changed" date="2026-06-24" type="official">
## What we changed

- kb-search's cache settings are now reviewed like code, and a time-to-live above 24 hours needs the Search team's approval.
- Each kb-search result now carries the date the article was last updated, and `research_agent` includes it when it cites a source.
- Reports produced during the affected week were flagged to their readers.

Based on the incident records and root cause analysis, here are the recurring patterns I found across our three incidents:

## **INC-2041** (2026-04-08) - billing_agent unable to issue invoices
**Root Cause:** An expired intermediate certificate in auth-service caused every request to payments-gateway to timeout, which then timed out before returning an error. The `billing_agent` incorrectly treated these timeouts as transient errors and kept retrying until it hit its step limit [D09:2].

## **INC-2067** (2026-06-15) - research_agent returning outdated results
**Root Cause:** A configuration change increased kb-search's cache time-to-live from 7 hours to 7 days. Cached answers returned versions of articles from when they were first cached, not their current state. Monitoring couldn't catch this because cached responses are fast and never fail—they just return stale data [D10:1][D10:0].

## **INC-2093** (2026-08-27) - registry outage during database failover
**Root Cause:** A primary registry-db host failed a disk check, triggering a failover that caused `RegistryUnreachable` alert and cascading failures affecting both `support_agent` and `triage_agent` [D11:1].

---

## **Common Recurring Causes:**

1. **Configuration Changes Without Validation:** INC-2067 shows a pattern where infrastructure parameter changes (cache TTL) weren't rigorously validated before deployment.

2. **Error Treatment Misconceptions:** INC-2041 demonstrates agents treating legitimate errors (certificate expiration) as transient retriable failures.

3. **Infrastructure Reliability Issues:** Disk failures and failover processes (INC-2093) can cause cascading agent failures.

4. **Missing Observability Gaps:** In INC-2067, no metrics existed to detect stale search results—only manual discovery revealed the problem.

### Batch jobs

For batch jobs it makes sense to page if the batch job has not succeeded
recently enough, and this will cause user-visible problems.

This should generally be at least enough time for 2 full runs of the batch job.
For a job that runs every 4 hours and takes an hour, 10 hours would be a

job more frequently, as a single failure should not require human intervention.

`research_agent` finds its sources through kb-search. On 2026-06-15 a config change set the kb-search cache's time-to-live to 7 days instead of 7 hours. <source id="D10:3" doc="D10" title="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results" section="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results > What we changed" date="2026-06-24" type="official">
## What we changed

- kb-search's cache settings are now reviewed like code, and a time-to-live above 24 hours needs the Search team's approval.

Based on my search through incident reports and documentation, here are the root causes that have run through our incidents so far:

**INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results** [D10:0]
- **Root cause**: A configuration change set kb-search's cache time-to-live from 7 hours to 7 days, causing articles to return versions from when they were first cached instead of updated versions
- **Impact**: Knowledge base answers drifted further out of date over several days; user noticed policy changed 4 days earlier
- **Common theme**: Configuration changes without proper review processes or approval requirements

**INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices** [D09:2]
- **Root cause**: An intermediate certificate in auth-service expired at 06:00, causing payments-gateway timeout checks before it would talk to callers. The billing_agent treated timeouts as transient and retried until its step limit ran out
- **Impact**: Unable to issue invoices due to certificate chain expiration
- **Common themes**: Certificate management issues, authentication service failures causing downstream retry storms

**INC-2093: registry outage during database failover** [D11:1]
- **Root cause**: Primary registry-db host failed a disk check at 14:10, triggering automatic failover. The standby finished catching up and services recovered by 15:05
- **Impact**: Registry went unreachable; support_sessions began failing; 212 tickets queued because triage_agent couldn't hand them over
- **Common themes**: Infrastructure reliability issues, database failover procedures

**Recurring patterns across incidents:**
1. **Configuration changes without governance** (TTL increase without approval)
2. **Authentication/certificate management** failures causing cascading timeouts
3. **Infrastructure component failures** (disk failures) triggering automated failovers that can impact dependent services
4. **Retry storms** when services treat transient errors as retries rather than failures

Based on my search through incident reports and documentation, here are the root causes that have run through our incidents so far:

**INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results** [D10:0]
- **Root cause**: A configuration change set kb-search's cache time-to-live from 7 hours to 7 days, causing articles to return versions from when they were first cached instead of updated versions
- **Impact**: Knowledge base answers drifted further out of date over several days; user noticed policy changed 4 days earlier
- **Common theme**: Configuration changes without proper review processes or approval requirements

**INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices** [D09:2]
- **Root cause**: An intermediate certificate in auth-service expired at 06:00, causing payments-gateway timeout checks before it would talk to callers. The billing_agent treated timeouts as transient and retried until its step limit ran out
- **Impact**: Unable to issue invoices due to certificate chain expiration
- **Common themes**: Certificate management issues, authentication service failures causing downstream retry storms

**INC-2093: registry outage during database failover** [D11:1]
- **Root cause**: Primary registry-db host failed a disk check at 14:10, triggering automatic failover. The standby finished catching up and services recovered by 15:05
- **Impact**: Registry went unreachable; support_sessions began failing; 212 tickets queued because triage_agent couldn't hand them over
- **Common themes**: Infrastructure reliability issues, database failover procedures

**Recurring patterns across incidents:**
1. **Configuration changes without governance** (TTL increase without approval)
2. **Authentication/certificate management** failures causing cascading timeouts
3. **Infrastructure component failures** (disk failures) triggering automated failovers that can impact dependent services
4. **Retry storms** when services treat transient errors as retries rather than failures

## Step 1: Check the target is allowed

<source id="D01:5" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Updating an agent" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Updating an agent

`PATCH /agents/{agent_id}` changes one or more of `model`, `tier`, `owner` and `status`. Send only the fields you're changing. It needs a `write` key; a `read` key gets `REG-1004`.

```bash
curl -X PATCH https://registry.internal.example/v2/agents/research_agent \
  -H "X-Registry-Key: $REGISTRY_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model": "claude-sonnet"}'
```

A change takes effect on the agent's next session, not in the middle of one that's running. Setting `status` to `paused` stops new sessions from starting; `retired` also hides the agent from the default listing.
</source>

### Silence Expiry

Silences have:
- `StartsAt`, `EndsAt` - The active time range
- `ExpiresAt` - When to garbage collect (EndsAt + retention period)
- `UpdatedAt` - For conflict resolution during merge

Each instance independently:
- Evaluates silence state (pending/active/expired) based on current time
- Garbage collects expired silences past their retention period
- The GC is local only (no gossip) since all instances converge to the same decision
</source>
