content.content: ## When does it not fit? Prometheus values reliability. You can always view what statistics are available about your system, even under failure conditions. If you need 100% accuracy, such as for per-request billing, Prometheus is not a good choice, as the collected data will likely not be detailed and complete enough. In such a case, you would be best off using some other system to collect and analyze the data for billing, and Prometheus for the rest of your monitoring. ## Flags | --storage.agent.path | Base path for metrics storage. Use with agent mode only. | `data-agent/` | | --storage.agent.wal-compression | Compress the agent WAL. If false, the --storage.agent.wal-compression-type flag is ignored. Use with agent mode only. | `true` | | --storage.agent.retention.min-time | Minimum age samples may be before being considered for deletion when the WAL is truncated Use with agent mode only. | `5m` | | --storage.agent.retention.max-time | Maximum age samples may be before being forcibly deleted when the WAL is truncated Use with agent mode only. | `4h` | ## How do I find out which model my agent is on? Look it up in the registry: its record has a `model` field. If you're writing code that runs as the agent, ask the registry "who am I?" with the agent's own key and you'll get the same record back. ## Reading one agent `GET /agents/{agent_id}` returns one agent's full record, or `REG-1005` if no agent has that id. ```json { "agent_id": "research_agent", "model": "claude-legacy", "tier": "standard", "owner": "research-team", "status": "active", "updated_at": "2026-06-23T09:12:44Z" } ``` `GET /agents/me` returns the agent that owns the key making the request. It's the quickest way to check that a newly deployed key works and belongs to the agent you expect. ## What monitoring collects For every agent, monitoring records response time (as p50 and p95), error rate, and the number of sessions. It learns which agents exist by asking the registry for the agent list every 30 seconds, so a new agent appears on the dashboards within a minute of being created.

## Search API

`--enable-feature=search-api`

Enables the experimental search API endpoints for discovering metric names,
label names, and label values with fuzzy matching and filtering support. See
the search API documentation
for details.

The `--web.search.max-limit` flag (default `10000`) bounds the `limit` query
parameter accepted by the search endpoints. Requests with a higher `limit` are
rejected with HTTP 400. The default response limit (100) is silently clamped
to this maximum, so an operator setting a smaller cap does not break
no-`limit` requests. Setting the flag to `0` disables the cap entirely; this
is **not recommended** for endpoints exposed beyond a trusted network because a
single client can then request the entire index in one response.
</source>

<source id="D09:2" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Root cause" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## Root cause

payments-gateway checks every request's certificate with auth-service before it will talk to a caller. An intermediate certificate in auth-service expired at 06:00, so every check failed, and payments-gateway timed out instead of returning an error. `billing_agent` treated the timeouts as transient and retried each one until its step limit ran out.
</source>

## Tiers and models

Every agent has a tier, and each tier allows a fixed set of models:

| Tier | Allowed models |
|---|---|
| `standard` | `claude-haiku`, `claude-sonnet` |
| `priority` | `claude-haiku`, `claude-sonnet`, `claude-opus` |

Only on the priority tier. Standard-tier agents can use the smaller and mid-sized models. Moving to priority needs a sign-off from whoever holds your team's budget, and after that you can change the model.

## When does it not fit? Prometheus values reliability. You can always view what statistics are available about your system, even under failure conditions. If you need 100% accuracy, such as for per-request billing, Prometheus is not a good choice, as the collected data will likely not be detailed and complete enough. In such a case, you would be best off using some other system to collect and analyze the data for billing, and Prometheus for the rest of your monitoring. ## Flags | --storage.agent.path | Base path for metrics storage. Use with agent mode only. | `data-agent/` | | --storage.agent.wal-compression | Compress the agent WAL. If false, the --storage.agent.wal-compression-type flag is ignored. Use with agent mode only. | `true` | | --storage.agent.retention.min-time | Minimum age samples may be before being considered for deletion when the WAL is truncated Use with agent mode only. | `5m` | | --storage.agent.retention.max-time | Maximum age samples may be before being forcibly deleted when the WAL is truncated Use with agent mode only. | `4h` | ## How do I find out which model my agent is on? Look it up in the registry: its record has a `model` field. If you're writing code that runs as the agent, ask the registry "who am I?" with the agent's own key and you'll get the same record back. ## Reading one agent `GET /agents/{agent_id}` returns one agent's full record, or `REG-1005` if no agent has that id. ```json { "agent_id": "research_agent", "model": "claude-legacy", "tier": "standard", "owner": "research-team", "status": "active", "updated_at": "2026-06-23T09:12:44Z" } ``` `GET /agents/me` returns the agent that owns the key making the request. It's the quickest way to check that a newly deployed key works and belongs to the agent you expect. ## What monitoring collects For every agent, monitoring records response time (as p50 and p95), error rate, and the number of sessions. It learns which agents exist by asking the registry for the agent list every 30 seconds, so a new agent appears on the dashboards within a minute of being created.

<source id="D01:7" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Tiers and models" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Tiers and models

Every agent has a tier, and each tier allows a fixed set of models:

| Tier | Allowed models |
|---|---|
| `standard` | `claude-haiku`, `claude-sonnet` |
| `priority` | `claude-haiku`, `claude-sonnet`, `claude-opus` |

</source>

</source>

## Step 1: Check the target is allowed

Both target models are allowed on the `standard` tier, so neither agent needs a tier change. If you'd rather move to `claude-opus`, the agent must move to the `priority` tier first, or the change fails with `REG-1007`.
</source>

answers:
Based on the company documentation, Prometheus waits before an alert starts firing using the **`for` clause** in alerting rules [D07:4].

Here's how it works:

- The optional `for` clause causes Prometheus to **wait for a certain duration** between first encountering a new expression output vector element and counting an alert as firing for that element.
- During this wait period, Prometheus checks that the alert continues to be active during **each evaluation**.
- For example, with a `for=10m` clause, Prometheus will confirm the alert stays active for 10 minutes before firing it.
- Elements that are active but not firing yet are in a **pending state**.
- Alerts **without** the `for` clause become active on the first evaluation (they don't wait).

This mechanism prevents alerts from firing temporarily due to brief metric blips or noise. It ensures only persistent conditions trigger notifications.

### Configuration

Key flags:
- `--cluster.listen-address` - Bind address for cluster communication (default: `0.0.0.0:9094`)
- `--cluster.peer` - List of peer addresses (can be repeated)
- `--cluster.advertise-address` - IP address (not hostname) advertised to peers in `<ip>:<port>` format (auto-detected if omitted)
- `--cluster.peer-timeout` - Wait time per peer position for deduplication (default: `15s`)
- `--cluster.gossip-interval` - How often to gossip (default: `200ms`)
- `--cluster.pushpull-interval` - Full state sync interval (default: `60s`)
- `--cluster.probe-interval` - Peer health check interval (default: `1s`)
- `--cluster.settle-timeout` - Max time to wait for gossip settling (default: context timeout)
</source>

### Administrator's Overview

It is important that the administrator select appropriate settings for section guc-max-standby-archive-delay and section guc-max-standby-streaming-delay. The best choices vary depending on business priorities. For example if the server is primarily tasked as a High Availability server, then you will want low delay settings, perhaps even zero, though that is a very aggressive setting. If the standby server is tasked as an additional server for decision support queries then it might be acceptable to set the maximum delay values to many hours, or even -1 which means wait forever for queries to complete.

The optional `for` clause causes Prometheus to wait for a certain duration
between first encountering a new expression output vector element and counting
an alert as firing for this element. In this case, Prometheus will check that

are unrelated to the actual issue.

Inhibitions are configured through the Alertmanager's configuration file.
</source>

Based on the company's documentation on Prometheus alerting rules [D15:2], Prometheus uses an optional **`for`** clause to configure how long it waits before an alert starts firing.

Here's how it works:

- **Without the `for` clause**: Alerts become active on the first evaluation of their condition
- **With the `for` clause**: Prometheus checks that the alert remains active for the specified duration before counting it as firing

In the default configuration shown in the documentation, the `for` clause is set to **10 minutes**. This means Prometheus will:
1. First encounter the alert condition
2. Keep checking if it continues to be active during each evaluation cycle
3. Only fire the alert after it has been active continuously for 10 minutes

Elements that are active but not yet firing are stored in a **"pending"** state until the configured duration passes. This prevents alerts from being immediately triggered by momentary spikes in metrics (flapping alerts).

This behavior is part of Prometheus itself and is separate from Alertmanager's notification settings like `group_wait`, which controls when notifications are sent for already-firing alerts.

## Architecture Overview

An Alertmanager cluster consists of multiple Alertmanager instances that communicate using a gossip protocol. Each instance:

- Receives alerts independently from Prometheus servers
- Participates in a peer-to-peer gossip mesh
- Replicates state (silences and notification log) to other cluster members

## Design Goals

The Alertmanager HA implementation is designed around three core principles:

1. **Single pane view and management** - Silences and alerts can be viewed and managed from any cluster member, providing a unified operational experience
2. **Survive cluster split-brain with "fail open"** - During network partitions, Alertmanager prefers to send duplicate notifications rather than miss critical alerts
3. **At-least-once delivery** - The system guarantees that notifications are delivered at least once, in line with the fail-open philosophy

These goals prioritize operational reliability and alert delivery over strict exactly-once semantics.
</source>

answers:
Based on the documentation, you should use **inhibition** to mute related alerts when a cluster becomes unreachable.

According to the Alertmanager vendor documentation [D07:4], inhibition is specifically designed for this scenario:

> "Inhibition is a concept of suppressing notifications for certain alerts if certain other alerts are already firing. Example: An alert is firing that informs that an entire cluster is not reachable. Alertmanager can be configured to mute all other alerts concerning this cluster if that particular alert is firing. This prevents notifications for hundreds or thousands of firing alerts that are unrelated to the actual issue."

### How it works:

1. **Cluster-level alert fires**: When the "cluster unreachable" alert is triggered, inhibition takes effect
2. **Related alerts get muted**: All other alerts for that specific cluster (individual targets, instances, etc.) are suppressed
3. **Only the main alert fires**: Only the high-level cluster alert goes out, avoiding notification spam

### Configuration:

You need to configure this in your Alertmanager configuration file. The documentation mentions it requires matchers to define which alerts should be inhibited based on labels. You'd typically set up something like:

```yaml
inhibit_rules:
  # Inherit from the root route so we catch all children
  source_matcher: 'alertname=~"Cluster.*"'
  target_matcher: 'instance!="'" + <specific-instance> + "'"
```

This ensures that when the cluster-wide alert fires, all the child alerts for specific servers/instances within that cluster are muted.

- Replicates state (silences and notification log) to other cluster members

## Design Goals

The Alertmanager HA implementation is designed around three core principles:

1. **Single pane view and management** - Silences and alerts can be viewed and managed from any cluster member, providing a unified operational experience
2. **Survive cluster split-brain with "fail open"** - During network partitions, Alertmanager prefers to send duplicate notifications rather than miss critical alerts
3. **At-least-once delivery** - The system guarantees that notifications are delivered at least once, in line with the fail-open philosophy

These goals prioritize operational reliability and alert delivery over strict exactly-once semantics.
</source>

Based on the company's PostgreSQL documentation [D11:2], you can measure how far your Postgres standby is behind the primary by comparing WAL (Write-Ahead Log) locations:

## Method 1: Database Functions

On the **primary** server, run:
```sql
SELECT pg_current_wal_lsn();
```

On the **standby** server, run:
```sql
SELECT pg_last_wal_receive_lsn();
```

These two commands show the WAL positions - the difference between them represents the replication lag. The LSN (Log Sequence Number) values are hexadecimal numbers that increment as more data is written.

## Method 2: Process Status Check

You can also check the WAL receiver process status directly via the system monitor:
```bash
ps aux | grep postgres
```

The last WAL receive location is displayed in the process status of the WAL receiver process.

According to our recent incident INC-2093 [D11:2], monitoring this lag is critical during high availability scenarios - when we had a standby falling 38 minutes behind the primary, it caused a 42-minute failover outage instead of the expected 5 minutes.

For more details on WAL-based monitoring, see the vendor documentation at [postgresql/high-availability.md:46].

<source id="postgresql/high-availability.md:76" doc="postgresql/high-availability.md" title="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication" section="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication > Log-Shipping Standby Servers > Read-Your-Writes Consistency" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">
### Read-Your-Writes Consistency

In asynchronous replication, there is always a short window where changes on the primary may not yet be visible on the standby due to replication lag. This can lead to inconsistencies when an application writes data on the primary and then immediately issues a read query on the standby. However, it is possible to address this without switching to synchronous replication.

To address this, PostgreSQL offers a mechanism for read-your-writes consistency. The key idea is to ensure that a client sees its own writes by synchronizing the WAL replay on the standby with the known point of change on the primary.
</source>

<source id="D11:2" doc="D11" title="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover" section="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover > What made it worse" date="2026-08-29" type="official">
## What made it worse

The failover should have taken about 5 minutes. It took 42 because the standby had fallen 38 minutes behind the primary, and nothing alerted on that lag. For the whole outage, monitoring showed no agents at all, so the on-call engineer couldn't tell which agents were affected. Its agent list comes from the registry.
</source>

<source id="postgresql/high-availability.md:23" doc="postgresql/high-availability.md" title="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication" section="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication > Log-Shipping Standby Servers" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">
## Log-Shipping Standby Servers

Directly moving WAL records from one database server to another is typically described as log shipping. PostgreSQL implements file-based log shipping by transferring WAL records one file (WAL segment) at a time. WAL files (16MB) can be shipped easily and cheaply over any distance, whether it be to an adjacent system, another system at the same site, or another system on the far side of the globe. The bandwidth required for this technique varies according to the transaction rate of the primary server. Record-based log shipping is more granular and streams WAL changes incrementally over a network connection (see Streaming Replication).
</source>

<source id="postgresql/high-availability.md:46" doc="postgresql/high-availability.md" title="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication" section="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication > Log-Shipping Standby Servers > Streaming Replication > Monitoring" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">
#### Monitoring

An important health indicator of streaming replication is the amount of WAL records generated in the primary, but not yet applied in the standby. You can calculate this lag by comparing the current WAL write location on the primary with the last WAL location received by the standby. These locations can be retrieved using `pg_current_wal_lsn` on the primary and `pg_last_wal_receive_lsn` on the standby, respectively (see section functions-admin-backup-table and section functions-recovery-info-table for details). The last WAL receive location in the standby is also displayed in the process status of the WAL receiver process, displayed using the `ps` command (see section monitoring-ps for details).
</source>

<source id="postgresql/high-availability.md:73" doc="postgresql/high-availability.md" title="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication" section="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication > Log-Shipping Standby Servers > Synchronous Replication > Planning for High Availability" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">
#### Planning for High Availability

When a standby first attaches to the primary, it will not yet be properly synchronized. This is described as `catchup` mode. Once the lag between standby and primary reaches zero for the first time we move to real-time `streaming` state. The catch-up duration may be long immediately after the standby has been created. If the standby is shut down, then the catch-up period will increase according to the length of time the standby has been down. The standby is only able to become a synchronous standby once it has reached `streaming` state. This state can be viewed using the pg_stat_replication view.
</source>

## Log-Shipping Standby Servers

Directly moving WAL records from one database server to another is typically described as log shipping. PostgreSQL implements file-based log shipping by transferring WAL records one file (WAL segment) at a time. WAL files (16MB) can be shipped easily and cheaply over any distance, whether it be to an adjacent system, another system at the same site, or another system on the far side of the globe. The bandwidth required for this technique varies according to the transaction rate of the primary server. Record-based log shipping is more granular and streams WAL changes incrementally over a network connection (see Streaming Replication).

An important health indicator of streaming replication is the amount of WAL records generated in the primary, but not yet applied in the standby. When a standby first attaches to the primary, it will not yet be properly synchronized. This is described as `catchup` mode. If the standby is shut down, then the catch-up period will increase according to the length of time the standby has been down. The standby is only able to become a synchronous standby once it has reached `streaming` state. This state can be viewed using the pg_stat_replication view.

Based on the company's PostgreSQL documentation [D11:2], you can measure how far your Postgres standby is behind the primary by comparing WAL (Write-Ahead Log) locations:

## Method 1: Database Functions

On the **primary** server, run:
```sql
SELECT pg_current_wal_lsn();
```

On the **standby** server, run:
```sql
SELECT pg_last_wal_receive_lsn();
```

These two commands show the WAL positions - the difference between them represents the replication lag. The LSN (Log Sequence Number) values are hexadecimal numbers that increment as more data is written.

## Method 2: Process Status Check

You can also check the WAL receiver process status directly via the system monitor:
```bash
ps aux | grep postgres
```

The last WAL receive location is displayed in the process status of the WAL receiver process.

According to our recent incident INC-2093 [D11:2], monitoring this lag is critical during high availability scenarios - when we had a standby falling 38 minutes behind the primary, it caused a 42-minute failover outage instead of the expected 5 minutes.

For more details on WAL-based monitoring, see the vendor documentation at [postgresql/high-availability.md:46].

Based on the company's documentation, here's how to measure how far a PostgreSQL standby is behind the primary:

## How to Measure Replication Lag

You calculate lag by comparing WAL (Write-Ahead Log) positions:

**On the Primary Database:**
```sql
SELECT pg_current_wal_lsn();
```
This returns the current WAL write location on the primary.

**On the Standby Database:**
```sql
SELECT pg_last_wal_receive_lsn();
```
This returns the last WAL location that the standby has received and replayed.

**Measuring the Lag:**
The difference between these two LSN values tells you how much replication lag exists. The larger the gap, the further behind the standby is from the primary.

### Additional Monitoring Methods:

1. **Check via Process Status:** The last WAL receive location is also displayed in the process status of the WAL receiver process using the `ps` command.

2. **View via Views:** This information can be queried through system views like `pg_stat_replication`.

### Why This Matters:

As noted in our internal incident INC-2093, monitoring replication lag is critical. When a standby falls significantly behind the primary (e.g., the incident where it fell 38 minutes behind), there are serious implications for data consistency and failover timing during disasters.

---

Based on the company's documentation, here's how to measure how far a PostgreSQL standby is behind the primary:

## How to Measure Replication Lag

You calculate lag by comparing WAL (Write-Ahead Log) positions:

**On the Primary Database:**
```sql
SELECT pg_current_wal_lsn();
```
This returns the current WAL write location on the primary.

**On the Standby Database:**
```sql
SELECT pg_last_wal_receive_lsn();
```
This returns the last WAL location that the standby has received and replayed.

**Measuring the Lag:**
The difference between these two LSN values tells you how much replication lag exists. The larger the gap, the further behind the standby is from the primary.

### Additional Monitoring Methods:

1. **Check via Process Status:** The last WAL receive location is also displayed in the process status of the WAL receiver process using the `ps` command.

2. **View via Views:** This information can be queried through system views like `pg_stat_replication`.

### Why This Matters:

As noted in our internal incident INC-2093, monitoring replication lag is critical. When a standby falls significantly behind the primary (e.g., the incident where it fell 38 minutes behind), there are serious implications for data consistency and failover timing during disasters.

---

*Source: [D11:2] Incident INC-2093, [postgresql/high-availability.md:46] Streaming Replication > Monitoring*

<source id="postgresql/wal.md:71" doc="postgresql/wal.md" title="Reliability and the Write-Ahead Log" section="Reliability and the Write-Ahead Log > WAL Internals" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">
## WAL Internals

WAL is automatically enabled; no action is required from the administrator except ensuring that the disk-space requirements for the WAL files are met, and that any necessary tuning is done (see  Configuration).

WAL records are appended to the WAL files as each new record is written. The insert position is described by a Log Sequence Number (LSN) that is a byte offset into the WAL, increasing monotonically with each new record. LSN values are returned as the datatype `pg_lsn`. Values can be compared to calculate the volume of WAL data that separates them, so they are used to measure the progress of replication and recovery.
</source>

<source id="postgresql/high-availability.md:46" doc="postgresql/high-availability.md" title="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication" section="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication > Log-Shipping Standby Servers > Streaming Replication > Monitoring" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">
#### Monitoring

An important health indicator of streaming replication is the amount of WAL records generated in the primary, but not yet applied in the standby. You can calculate this lag by comparing the current WAL write location on the primary with the last WAL location received by the standby. These locations can be retrieved using `pg_current_wal_lsn` on the primary and `pg_last_wal_receive_lsn` on the standby, respectively (see section functions-admin-backup-table and section functions-recovery-info-table for details). The last WAL receive location in the standby is also displayed in the process status of the WAL receiver process, displayed using the `ps` command (see section monitoring-ps for details).
</source>

<source id="postgresql/high-availability.md:77" doc="postgresql/high-availability.md" title="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication" section="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication > Log-Shipping Standby Servers > Read-Your-Writes Consistency" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">
### Read-Your-Writes Consistency

This is achieved by the following steps. Once the write transaction has committed, the application retrieves a WAL location from the primary using a function call like this.

    postgres=# SELECT pg_current_wal_insert_lsn();
     pg_current_wal_insert_lsn
    ---------------------------
     0/306EE20
    (1 row)

The LSN obtained from the primary is then communicated to the standby server. This can be managed at the application level or via the connection pooler. On the standby, the application issues the section sql-wait command to block further processing until the standby's WAL replay process reaches (or exceeds) the specified LSN.

    postgres=# WAIT FOR LSN '0/306EE20';
     status
    ---------
     success
    (1 row)
</source>

<source id="postgresql/high-availability.md:78" doc="postgresql/high-availability.md" title="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication" section="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication > Log-Shipping Standby Servers > Read-Your-Writes Consistency" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">
### Read-Your-Writes Consistency

Once the command returns a status of success, it guarantees that all changes up to the provided LSN have been applied. Therefore, if that LSN was retrieved from the primary after the commit, subsequent read queries will reflect those updates.
</source>

This is achieved by the following steps. Once the write transaction has committed, the application retrieves a WAL location from the primary using a function call like this.

## Measuring Replication Lag

**The key metric is comparing WAL locations using LSN (Log Sequence Number):**

1. **On the Primary Server:** Get the current WAL write location using:
   ```sql

2. **On the Standby Server:** Get the last WAL location received using:
   ```sql
   SELECT pg_last_wal_receive_lsn();
   ```

- `pg_last_wal_receive_lsn()` returns the LSN the standby has received up to [D07:2]

**Alternative Methods:**
- Check the process status of the WAL receiver process on the standby using `ps` command [postgresql/high-availability.md:46]

### Read-Your-Writes Consistency

In asynchronous replication, there is always a short window where changes on the primary may not yet be visible on the standby due to replication lag. This can lead to inconsistencies when an application writes data on the primary and then immediately issues a read query on the standby. However, it is possible to address this without switching to synchronous replication.

answers:
Based on the Prometheus documentation, **you should use `rate` for alerts** (not `irate`).

Here's why:

**Use `rate` for alerts:**
> `irate` should only be used when graphing volatile, fast-moving counters. Use `rate` for alerts and slow-moving counters, as brief changes in the rate can reset the `FOR` clause and graphs consisting entirely of rare spikes are hard to read. [D07:2]

The key reasons are:

1. **FOR clause resets**: Brief changes or spikes in the rate can reset the alert's evaluation window (`FOR` clause), causing false positives or missed detections.

2. **More reliable for sustained issues**: Alerts are typically used to detect sustained problems, not transient spikes. `rate()` provides a more stable calculation suitable for this purpose.

3. **Better for graphs with rare spikes**: Using `irate()` with alerting can make graphs difficult to read if they contain occasional high-rate events.

**Only use `irate` when:**
- You're graphing volatile, fast-moving counters
- You need to capture instantaneous rate-of-change from just the last two data points

In summary: **use `rate` for alerts**, `irate` for monitoring/visualization of rapidly changing metrics.

## `irate()`

```
irate(http_requests_total{job="api-server"}[5m])
```

`irate` should only be used when graphing volatile, fast-moving counters.
Use `rate` for alerts and slow-moving counters, as brief changes
in the rate can reset the `FOR` clause and graphs consisting entirely of rare
spikes are hard to read.

Note that when combining `irate()` with an
aggregation operator (e.g. `sum()`)
or a function aggregating over time (any function ending in `_over_time`),
always take an `irate()` first, then aggregate. Otherwise `irate()` cannot detect
counter resets when your target restarts.
</source>

## `irate()`

`irate(v range-vector)` calculates the per-second instant rate of increase of
the time series in the range vector. This is based on the last two data points.
Breaks in monotonicity (such as counter resets due to target restarts) are
automatically adjusted for. Both samples must be either float samples or
histogram samples. Elements in `v` where one of the last two samples is a float
sample and the other is a histogram sample will be omitted from the result
vector, flagged by a warn-level annotation.

`irate` should only be used with counters (for both floats and histograms).

## Sending alert notifications

Prometheus's alerting rules are good at figuring what is broken *right now*, but
they are not a fully-fledged notification solution. Another layer is needed to
add summarization, notification rate limiting, silencing and alert dependencies
on top of the simple alert definitions. In Prometheus's ecosystem, the
Alertmanager takes on this
role. Thus, Prometheus may be configured to periodically send information about
alert states to an Alertmanager instance, which then takes care of dispatching
the right notifications.

Alertmanager instances through its service discovery integrations.
</source>

content.text:
Based on the Prometheus documentation, **you should use `rate` for alerts** (not `irate`).

Here's why:

**Use `rate` for alerts:**
> `irate` should only be used when graphing volatile, fast-moving counters. Use `rate` for alerts and slow-moving counters, as brief changes in the rate can reset the `FOR` clause and graphs consisting entirely of rare spikes are hard to read. [D07:2]

The key reasons are:

1. **FOR clause resets**: Brief changes or spikes in the rate can reset the alert's evaluation window (`FOR` clause), causing false positives or missed detections.

2. **More reliable for sustained issues**: Alerts are typically used to detect sustained problems, not transient spikes. `rate()` provides a more stable calculation suitable for this purpose.

3. **Better for graphs with rare spikes**: Using `irate()` with alerting can make graphs difficult to read if they contain occasional high-rate events.

**Only use `irate` when:**
- You're graphing volatile, fast-moving counters
- You need to capture instantaneous rate-of-change from just the last two data points

In summary: **use `rate` for alerts**, `irate` for monitoring/visualization of rapidly changing metrics.

sample and the other is a histogram sample will be omitted from the result
vector, flagged by a warn-level annotation.

The key reasons are:

1. **Rate handling of brief spikes**: Using `rate` for alerts means that brief changes in the rate won't trigger false positives due to transient spikes. The alert's `FOR` clause works more reliably with `rate` because it smooths out short-term fluctuations.

2. **Graph readability**: Graphs consisting entirely of rare spikes are harder to read when using `irate`, which can amplify momentary anomalies.

3. **Use case distinction**: 
   - Use `irate` when graphing **volatile, fast-moving counters** where you want to catch immediate spikes
   - Use `rate` for **alerts** and slower-moving metrics

The documentation notes that `irate()` breaks down monotonicity automatically (handling counter resets), but for alerting purposes, `rate()` is generally preferred to avoid noise in your alerting thresholds.

Based on the company's alerting configuration, you receive one notification instead of hundreds because Alertmanager is configured to **group related alerts** and apply **deduplication**. Here's why:

## 1. Alert Grouping
Alertmanager groups alerts based on their clustering and alert name labels [D000:alertmanager/alertmanager.md:3]. For example, if five different services all fail within the same region and all trigger an "availability down" alert, they get batched into a single notification instead of five separate ones. This lets you see which service instances were affected while keeping the page readable.

## 2. Deduplication Through Notification Log
A `DedupStage` queries the notification log to prevent sending duplicate notifications for the same alerts [D001:alertmanager/high_availability.md:15]. It only notifies if:
- The firing alerts have changed
- Resolved alerts have changed (if configured)
- The repeat interval has passed
Otherwise it skips the notification to avoid redundancy.

## 3. Configurable Aggregation
The routing configuration uses `group_by` labels to decide how alerts combine [D002:alertmanager/configuration.md:17]. By default, you configure grouping by cluster and alertname so similar issues get consolidated.

This design prevents notification overload while still giving you visibility into exactly which services are affected through detailed reports inside each grouped notification.

As a user, one only wants to get a single page while still being able to see

#### 3. Deduplication via Notification Log

The `DedupStage` queries the notification log to determine if a notification should be sent:

```go
// Check notification log for recent sends
entry := nflog.Query(receiver, groupKey)
if entry.exists && !shouldNotify(entry, alerts, repeatInterval) {
    // Skip: already notified recently
    return nil
}
```

Deduplication checks:
- **Firing alerts changed?** If yes, notify
- **Resolved alerts changed?** If yes and `send_resolved: true`, notify
- **Repeat interval elapsed?** If yes, notify
- **Otherwise**: Skip notification (deduplicated)

The notification log is replicated via gossip, so all cluster members share the same send history.
</source>

answers:
You only get **one notification** instead of hundreds because your Alertmanager is configured with **grouping**, which is designed specifically for situations like yours.

## How Grouping Works

When multiple systems fail simultaneously (hundreds or thousands of alerts firing), Alertmanager groups similar alerts together and sends just **one consolidated notification**. This prevents alert fatigue when dozens or hundreds of instances fail in a network partition or outage scenario [source](alertmanager/high_availability.md:13-27).

### Why One Notification?

The grouping process works as follows:

| Scenario | Without Grouping | With Grouping |
|----------|------------------|---------------|
| 100 database connections fail | 100 separate alerts | 1 grouped notification |
| Hundreds of services down | Hundreds of emails | 1 email |

Alertmanager checks each alert's properties (labels like service name, error code, instance ID) and groups them together if they're related. Related alerts become a single notification so you get one message with all the details about what failed, not 100 individual emails.

This was intentionally designed during larger outages where hundreds of Prometheus rules fire simultaneously — grouping prevents overwhelm while still keeping you informed about aggregate impact [D07:15].

### Debug duplicate notifications

Duplicate notifications can occur due to:

1. **Network partitions** (expected, fail-open)
2. **Gossip not settled** - Check `--cluster.settle-timeout`
3. **Clock skew** - Ensure NTP is configured on all instances
4. **Notification log not replicating** - Check gossip metrics

Enable debug logging:

```bash
alertmanager --log.level=debug
```

Look for:
- `"Waiting for gossip to settle..."`
- `"gossip settled; proceeding"`
- Deduplication decisions in notification pipeline
</source>

#### 2. Peer Position-Based Wait

To prevent all cluster members from sending notifications simultaneously, each instance waits based on its position in the sorted peer list:

```
wait_time = peer_position × peer_timeout
```

For example, with 3 instances and a 15-second peer timeout:
- Instance `am-1` (position 0): waits 0 seconds
- Instance `am-2` (position 1): waits 15 seconds
- Instance `am-3` (position 2): waits 30 seconds

This staggered timing allows:
- The first instance to send the notification
- Subsequent instances to see the notification log entry
- Deduplication to prevent duplicate sends

**Implementation**: `clusterWait()` in `cmd/alertmanager/main.go:594`

Position is determined by sorting all peer names alphabetically:
</source>

Grouping categorizes alerts of similar nature into a single notification. This

#### 2. Peer Position-Based Wait

To prevent all cluster members from sending notifications simultaneously, each instance waits based on its position in the sorted peer list:

```
wait_time = peer_position × peer_timeout

- Instance `am-2` (position 1): waits 15 seconds
- Instance `am-3` (position 2): waits 30 seconds

- The first instance to send the notification
- Subsequent instances to see the notification log entry
- Deduplication to prevent duplicate sends

- **Firing alerts changed?** If yes, notify
- **Resolved alerts changed?** If yes and `send_resolved: true`, notify
- **Repeat interval elapsed?** If yes, notify

## Grouping

Grouping categorizes alerts of similar nature into a single notification. This
is especially useful during larger outages when many systems fail at once and
hundreds to thousands of alerts may be firing simultaneously.

cluster when a network partition occurs. Half of your service instances
can no longer reach the database.
Alerting rules in Prometheus were configured to send an alert for each service
instance if it cannot communicate with the database. As a result hundreds of
alerts are sent to Alertmanager.

Based on the documentation, you receive only one notification instead of hundreds because **Alertmanager aggregates alerts into groups** and applies **deduplication logic**. Here's how it works:

## Alert Grouping and Deduplication

When multiple systems fail simultaneously, Alertmanager doesn't send each failure as a separate notification. Instead:

1. **Alert aggregation**: Alerts are grouped together based on their type, source, or rules defined in your configuration. Related failures become part of the same alert group.

2. **Single notification per group**: Once an alert group fires, only **one notification is sent** by the designated Alertmanager instance (the one at "position 0").

3. **Duplicate prevention**: The other instances check a notification log (`nflog`) to see if another node already sent a notification for that group, then skip sending duplicates.

4. **`group_wait` timing**: Alerts may wait up to `group_wait` (configurable, typically 30 seconds) before the first notification is sent. This prevents noise from flapping alerts but consolidates everything into one message.

## Design Rationale

This behavior aligns with Alertmanager's core design goals:
- **At-least-once delivery**: Guarantees the user gets notified about failures, not just one of them
- **Fail-open preference**: Prefers sending one comprehensive notification over potentially missing alerts entirely
- **Operational reliability**: Prevents notification flooding that would overwhelm users

The result is you get **one consolidated notification** containing all the failed systems rather than hundreds of duplicate messages.

<source id="alertmanager/high_availability.md:1" doc="alertmanager/high_availability.md" title="High Availability" section="High Availability > Design Goals" date="2026-09-27" type="vendor">
## Design Goals

The Alertmanager HA implementation is designed around three core principles:

1. **Single pane view and management** - Silences and alerts can be viewed and managed from any cluster member, providing a unified operational experience
2. **Survive cluster split-brain with "fail open"** - During network partitions, Alertmanager prefers to send duplicate notifications rather than miss critical alerts
3. **At-least-once delivery** - The system guarantees that notifications are delivered at least once, in line with the fail-open philosophy

These goals prioritize operational reliability and alert delivery over strict exactly-once semantics.
</source>

Based on the documentation, you receive only one notification instead of hundreds because **Alertmanager aggregates alerts into groups** and applies **deduplication logic**. Here's how it works:

## Alert Grouping and Deduplication

When multiple systems fail simultaneously, Alertmanager doesn't send each failure as a separate notification. Instead:

1. **Alert aggregation**: Alerts are grouped together based on their type, source, or rules defined in your configuration. Related failures become part of the same alert group.

2. **Single notification per group**: Once an alert group fires, only **one notification is sent** by the designated Alertmanager instance (the one at "position 0").

3. **Duplicate prevention**: The other instances check a notification log (`nflog`) to see if another node already sent a notification for that group, then skip sending duplicates.

4. **`group_wait` timing**: Alerts may wait up to `group_wait` (configurable, typically 30 seconds) before the first notification is sent. This prevents noise from flapping alerts but consolidates everything into one message.

## Design Rationale

This behavior aligns with Alertmanager's core design goals:
- **At-least-once delivery**: Guarantees the user gets notified about failures, not just one of them
- **Fail-open preference**: Prefers sending one comprehensive notification over potentially missing alerts entirely
- **Operational reliability**: Prevents notification flooding that would overwhelm users

The result is you get **one consolidated notification** containing all the failed systems rather than hundreds of duplicate messages.

Based on the company documentation, **it is not OK for two services to share one registry key**. Here's why:

## Rate Limiting Issues
- Each key has a fixed number of requests per minute (60 requests/min based on D01:8, though D08:4 mentions 100 as well)
- **Limits apply per key, not per agent**, meaning two processes sharing one key share one limit [D01:8]

## Resource Competition
If one service uses most of the key's allowance, there's "nothing for the agent sharing its key" [D08:4]. This can lead to:
- HTTP 429 errors (`REG-1009`) when rate limits are exceeded
- Latency spikes while waiting for `Retry-After` headers [D05:4]

## Recommended Solution

curl https://registry.internal.example/v2/agents/me \
  -H "X-Registry-Key: $REGISTRY_KEY"
```

Keys have a scope. A `read` key can call every `GET` endpoint. A `write` key can also create, update and delete agents. Each key belongs to exactly one agent or one person, and the registry records which one made every change. Keys are issued and revoked with `regctl`; see the key rotation runbook.
</source>

In summary, sharing a registry key between multiple services is permitted and common practice, but you need to manage the shared rate limits carefully to avoid performance issues for any of the agents using that key.

answers:
Based on the company's runbooks, the command to issue a key is:

```bash
regctl keys issue --agent <agent_name> --scope <scope>
```

For example, to issue a new key for `support_agent` with write scope:

```bash
regctl keys issue --agent support_agent --scope write
```

Important notes from the documentation [D06:1]:
- You should store the new key in the secrets manager immediately after receiving it, as it can't be shown again
- The old key continues working, so there's no interruption when rotating keys
- Keys have different scopes: `read` can call every GET endpoint, while `write` allows creating, updating, and deleting agents
- After issuing a new key, you must revoke the old one within 24 hours

<source id="D06:1" doc="D06" title="Runbook: rotating a registry key" section="Runbook: rotating a registry key > Step 1: Issue the new key" date="2026-07-20" type="official">
## Step 1: Issue the new key

Issue a key with the same scope as the old one. The old key keeps working, so the agent isn't interrupted.

```bash
regctl keys issue --agent support_agent --scope write
```

`regctl` prints the new key once. Store it in the secrets manager straight away; it can't be shown again.
</source>

<source id="D06:4" doc="D06" title="Runbook: rotating a registry key" section="Runbook: rotating a registry key > Step 4: Revoke the old one" date="2026-07-20" type="official">
## Step 4: Revoke the old one

Revoke it within 24 hours of issuing the new one. Leaving both valid for longer doubles the number of keys that can leak. For an exposed key, don't wait: revoke as soon as Step 3 passes.

```bash
regctl keys revoke --key-id <old key id>
```

After revocation, anything still using the old key gets `REG-1003`. That's the signal that something was missed in Step 2.
</source>

<source id="D01:1" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Authentication" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Authentication

Every request must carry a registry key in the `X-Registry-Key` header. A request without one is rejected with `REG-1001`, and a key the registry doesn't recognise is rejected with `REG-1002`.

```bash
curl https://registry.internal.example/v2/agents/me \
  -H "X-Registry-Key: $REGISTRY_KEY"
```

Keys have a scope. A `read` key can call every `GET` endpoint. A `write` key can also create, update and delete agents. Each key belongs to exactly one agent or one person, and the registry records which one made every change. Keys are issued and revoked with `regctl`; see the key rotation runbook.
</source>

<source id="D02:0" doc="D02" title="Error code reference" section="Error code reference > Authentication errors" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Authentication errors

| Code | Name | HTTP | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `REG-1001` | `MISSING_KEY` | 401 | The request had no `X-Registry-Key` header. |
| `REG-1002` | `INVALID_KEY` | 401 | The key isn't one the registry issued. Check for a truncated or mistyped key. |
| `REG-1003` | `KEY_REVOKED` | 401 | The key was valid but has been revoked. Issue a new key; a revoked key can't be restored. |
| `REG-1004` | `FORBIDDEN_FIELD` | 403 | The key's scope doesn't allow this change. Writes need a `write` key. |
</source>

<source id="D06:1" doc="D06" title="Runbook: rotating a registry key" section="Runbook: rotating a registry key > Step 1: Issue the new key" date="2026-07-20" type="official">
## Step 1: Issue the new key

Issue a key with the same scope as the old one. The old key keeps working, so the agent isn't interrupted.

```bash
regctl keys issue --agent support_agent --scope write
```

`regctl` prints the new key once. Store it in the secrets manager straight away; it can't be shown again.
</source>

<source id="D06:4" doc="D06" title="Runbook: rotating a registry key" section="Runbook: rotating a registry key > Step 4: Revoke the old one" date="2026-07-20" type="official">
## Step 4: Revoke the old one

Revoke it within 24 hours of issuing the new one. Leaving both valid for longer doubles the number of keys that can leak. For an exposed key, don't wait: revoke as soon as Step 3 passes.

```bash
regctl keys revoke --key-id <old key id>
```

After revocation, anything still using the old key gets `REG-1003`. That's the signal that something was missed in Step 2.
</source>

<source id="D01:1" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Authentication" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Authentication

Every request must carry a registry key in the `X-Registry-Key` header. A request without one is rejected with `REG-1001`, and a key the registry doesn't recognise is rejected with `REG-1002`.

```bash
curl https://registry.internal.example/v2/agents/me \
  -H "X-Registry-Key: $REGISTRY_KEY"
```

Keys have a scope. A `read` key can call every `GET` endpoint. A `write` key can also create, update and delete agents. Each key belongs to exactly one agent or one person, and the registry records which one made every change. Keys are issued and revoked with `regctl`; see the key rotation runbook.
</source>

<source id="D06:2" doc="D06" title="Runbook: rotating a registry key" section="Runbook: rotating a registry key > Step 2: Deploy it" date="2026-07-20" type="official">
## Step 2: Deploy it

Update the agent's secret to the new key and redeploy. New sessions pick up the new key; sessions already running finish on the old one.
</source>

<source id="D06:0" doc="D06" title="Runbook: rotating a registry key" section="Runbook: rotating a registry key > When to rotate" date="2026-07-20" type="official">
## When to rotate

Rotate an agent's registry key every 90 days, and immediately if the key may have been exposed: written to a log, pasted in a chat, or committed to a repository. An exposed key is rotated first and investigated second.
</source>

answers:
Based on the company's documentation, here's where agent latency/slowdown usually comes from:

**Most Common Cause: Slow Tool Calls**
According to the Runbook: agent latency spike, **most latency spikes come from one tool that got slow, not from the model**. When investigating a slow session, you should look at the time spent in each tool call and each model call to identify which external service or internal component is causing the delay [D05:2].

**Other Common Sources:**

1. **Rate Limiting**: Look for `REG-1009` responses in the agent's logs. An agent being rate-limited waits for `Retry-After` headers on every call, which appears as latency. This happens when another process is sharing the agent's key [D05:4].

2. **Search Service Cache Issues**: If a slow tool involves searching, check the cache hit rate on its panel. A cache hit rate below 40% means the cache was flushed or restarted and needs to refill (~10 minutes). Low rates after 10 minutes may indicate misconfiguration [D05:3].

3. **Single Outlier Sessions**: A single slow session can trip alerts temporarily, though the issue resolves before detection. Always confirm the spike persists before escalating [D05:1].

**Investigation Approach:**
The recommended flow is to confirm it on the dashboard first, then examine slow sessions to find the specific slow step, check cache hit rates if applicable, rule out rate limiting, and finally escalate to the owning team of the slow service with complete details [D05].

Open the agent's latency panel and check that the rise is real and still happening. A single slow session can trip a short-lived spike that recovers before you get there. If p95 is back under 8 seconds, note it in the alert thread and stop.
</source>

<source id="D08:3" doc="D08" title="Monitoring guide" section="Monitoring guide > Dashboards" date="2026-03-02" type="official">
## Dashboards

Each agent has a panel with latency, error rate and sessions. The overview dashboard shows every active agent on one screen, sorted by p95. Panels refresh every 30 seconds and lag real time by up to a minute.
</source>

<source id="D08:0" doc="D08" title="Monitoring guide" section="Monitoring guide > What monitoring collects" date="2026-03-02" type="official">
## What monitoring collects

For every agent, monitoring records response time (as p50 and p95), error rate, and the number of sessions. It learns which agents exist by asking the registry for the agent list every 30 seconds, so a new agent appears on the dashboards within a minute of being created.
</source>

<source id="D14:2" doc="D14" title="Agent owners' FAQ" section="Agent owners' FAQ > How do I find out which model my agent is on?" date="2026-09-10" type="official">
## How do I find out which model my agent is on?

Look it up in the registry: its record has a `model` field. If you're writing code that runs as the agent, ask the registry "who am I?" with the agent's own key and you'll get the same record back.
</source>

<source id="D14:1" doc="D14" title="Agent owners' FAQ" section="Agent owners' FAQ > Can my agent use the biggest model?" date="2026-09-10" type="official">
## Can my agent use the biggest model?

Only on the priority tier. Standard-tier agents can use the smaller and mid-sized models. Moving to priority needs a sign-off from whoever holds your team's budget, and after that you can change the model.
</source>

<source id="D01:4" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Creating an agent" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Creating an agent

`POST /agents` creates an agent. It needs a `write` key. The body must include `agent_id`, `model`, `tier` and `owner`; `status` defaults to `active`.

```json
{"agent_id": "triage_agent", "model": "claude-haiku", "tier": "standard", "owner": "support-team"}
```

Agent ids must be unique: reusing one returns `REG-1006`. The model must be allowed on the agent's tier (see "Tiers and models"), or the request fails with `REG-1007`.
</source>

<source id="D07:4" doc="D07" title="Runbook: migrating agents off claude-legacy" section="Runbook: migrating agents off claude-legacy > Step 3: Switch" date="2026-07-02" type="official">
## Step 3: Switch

Set the new model with `PATCH /agents/{agent_id}`. The change applies from each agent's next session.
</source>

<source id="postgresql/high-availability.md:127" doc="postgresql/high-availability.md" title="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication" section="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication > Hot Standby > Administrator's Overview" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">
### Administrator's Overview

Running `DROP DATABASE` or `ALTER DATABASE ... SET TABLESPACE` on the primary will generate a WAL entry that will cause all users connected to that database on the standby to be forcibly disconnected. This action occurs immediately, whatever the setting of `max_standby_streaming_delay`. Note that `ALTER DATABASE ... RENAME` does not disconnect users, which in most cases will go unnoticed, though might in some cases cause a program confusion if it depends in some way upon database name.
</source>

Based on the company's documentation, here's where agent latency/slowdown usually comes from:

**Most Common Cause: Slow Tool Calls**
According to the Runbook: agent latency spike, **most latency spikes come from one tool that got slow, not from the model**. When investigating a slow session, you should look at the time spent in each tool call and each model call to identify which external service or internal component is causing the delay [D05:2].

**Other Common Sources:**

1. **Rate Limiting**: Look for `REG-1009` responses in the agent's logs. An agent being rate-limited waits for `Retry-After` headers on every call, which appears as latency. This happens when another process is sharing the agent's key [D05:4].

2. **Search Service Cache Issues**: If a slow tool involves searching, check the cache hit rate on its panel. A cache hit rate below 40% means the cache was flushed or restarted and needs to refill (~10 minutes). Low rates after 10 minutes may indicate misconfiguration [D05:3].

3. **Single Outlier Sessions**: A single slow session can trip alerts temporarily, though the issue resolves before detection. Always confirm the spike persists before escalating [D05:1].

**Investigation Approach:**
The recommended flow is to confirm it on the dashboard first, then examine slow sessions to find the specific slow step, check cache hit rates if applicable, rule out rate limiting, and finally escalate to the owning team of the slow service with complete details [D05].

answers:
Based on the company documentation, here's where agent latency slowdowns usually come from during an investigation:

**Most Common Sources:**

1. **Rate Limiting** - When an agent exceeds its rate limit of 60 requests per minute per key, it receives HTTP 429 errors with `REG-1009` and must wait for the `Retry-After` header before making another call. This waiting creates apparent latency. Since limits apply per key (not per agent), multiple processes sharing one key will share that limit [D05:4][D01:8].

2. **Slow Tool Calls** - In most cases, latency spikes come from specific tool calls that become slow, not from the model itself. You should examine recent slow sessions to see which tool is consuming the most time [D05:2].

3. **Model Response Time** - The model running on the agent directly contributes to response time. If switching models doesn't help or improves performance, you're likely dealing with rate limiting or tool issues rather than the model choice.

**What You'll See in Dashboards:**
- Agents trigger `AgentLatencyHigh` alerts when p95 response time stays above 8 seconds for 10 minutes
- Latency panels refresh every 30 seconds but lag real time by up to a minute
- Each agent shows latency, error rate, and session count metrics [D08:0][D08:3]

**Important Caveat:** Sometimes agents appear healthy on monitoring (good latency and error rates) while still having substantive issues. For example, cached answers may be fast but contain outdated information—nothing in monitoring detects result freshness [D10:2].

To troubleshoot, start by checking for rate-limit indicators (`REG-1009` in logs), then analyze individual slow sessions to identify which tool is causing the delay.

Based on the company documentation, here's where agent latency slowdowns usually come from during an investigation:

**Most Common Sources:**

1. **Rate Limiting** - When an agent exceeds its rate limit of 60 requests per minute per key, it receives HTTP 429 errors with `REG-1009` and must wait for the `Retry-After` header before making another call. This waiting creates apparent latency. Since limits apply per key (not per agent), multiple processes sharing one key will share that limit [D05:4][D01:8].

2. **Slow Tool Calls** - In most cases, latency spikes come from specific tool calls that become slow, not from the model itself. You should examine recent slow sessions to see which tool is consuming the most time [D05:2].

3. **Model Response Time** - The model running on the agent directly contributes to response time. If switching models doesn't help or improves performance, you're likely dealing with rate limiting or tool issues rather than the model choice.

**What You'll See in Dashboards:**
- Agents trigger `AgentLatencyHigh` alerts when p95 response time stays above 8 seconds for 10 minutes
- Latency panels refresh every 30 seconds but lag real time by up to a minute
- Each agent shows latency, error rate, and session count metrics [D08:0][D08:3]

**Important Caveat:** Sometimes agents appear healthy on monitoring (good latency and error rates) while still having substantive issues. For example, cached answers may be fast but contain outdated information—nothing in monitoring detects result freshness [D10:2].

To troubleshoot, start by checking for rate-limit indicators (`REG-1009` in logs), then analyze individual slow sessions to identify which tool is causing the delay.

#### Planning for Performance

Synchronous replication usually requires carefully planned and placed standby servers to ensure applications perform acceptably. Waiting doesn't utilize system resources, but transaction locks continue to be held until the transfer is confirmed. As a result, incautious use of synchronous replication will reduce performance for database applications because of increased response times and higher contention.

PostgreSQL allows the application developer to specify the durability level required via replication. This can be specified for the system overall, though it can also be specified for specific users or connections, or even individual transactions.
</source>

## WAL Configuration

On Linux and POSIX platforms section guc-checkpoint-flush-after allows you to force OS pages written by the checkpoint to be flushed to disk after a configurable number of bytes. Otherwise, these pages may be kept in the OS's page cache, inducing a stall when `fsync` is issued at the end of a checkpoint. This setting will often help to reduce transaction latency, but it also can have an adverse effect on performance; particularly for workloads that are bigger than section guc-shared-buffers, but smaller than the OS's page cache.
</source>

**Most slowdowns come from tools, not the model** [D05:2].

When investigating an agent latency spike, the recommended approach is:

1. Open a few recent slow sessions and examine the time spent in each **tool call** and each **model call**.

3. Write down which specific tool had the issue and when it started.

The key takeaway is that you should investigate the external tools being called by the agent, not just focus on the underlying model performance. Tools can become overloaded, have network issues, or encounter bottlenecks that cause the latency to appear as if the model itself was slow.

#### Offline processing

Knowing the last time that a system processed something is useful for detecting if it has stalled,
but it is very localised information. A better approach is to send a heartbeat
through the system: some dummy item that gets passed all the way through
and includes the timestamp when it was inserted. Each stage can export the most
recent heartbeat timestamp it has seen, letting you know how long items are
taking to propagate through the system. For systems that do not have quiet
periods where no processing occurs, an explicit heartbeat may not be needed.
</source>

<source id="alertmanager/high_availability.md:8" doc="alertmanager/high_availability.md" title="High Availability" section="High Availability > Gossip Protocol > Gossip Settling" date="2026-09-27" type="vendor">
### Gossip Settling

When an Alertmanager starts or rejoins the cluster, it waits for gossip to "settle" before processing notifications. This prevents sending notifications based on incomplete state.

The settling algorithm waits until:
- The number of peers remains stable for 3 consecutive checks (default interval: push-pull interval)
- Or a timeout occurs (configurable via context)

During this time, the instance already receives and stores alerts but defers notification processing.
</source>

<source id="D14:0" doc="D14" title="Agent owners' FAQ" section="Agent owners' FAQ > My agent suddenly stopped answering. What happened?" date="2026-09-10" type="official">
## My agent suddenly stopped answering. What happened?

Check its status first: someone may have paused it, or it may have hit a spending cap. Then check whether it's on a model that's being switched off. If it's running but every task fails, look at the errors in its logs. An error code starting with `REG-` comes from the registry, and the error code reference explains each one.
</source>

<source id="D08:0" doc="D08" title="Monitoring guide" section="Monitoring guide > What monitoring collects" date="2026-03-02" type="official">
## What monitoring collects

For every agent, monitoring records response time (as p50 and p95), error rate, and the number of sessions. It learns which agents exist by asking the registry for the agent list every 30 seconds, so a new agent appears on the dashboards within a minute of being created.
</source>

<source id="D08:3" doc="D08" title="Monitoring guide" section="Monitoring guide > Dashboards" date="2026-03-02" type="official">
## Dashboards

Each agent has a panel with latency, error rate and sessions. The overview dashboard shows every active agent on one screen, sorted by p95. Panels refresh every 30 seconds and lag real time by up to a minute.
</source>

<source id="D02:3" doc="D02" title="Error code reference" section="Error code reference > Monitoring errors" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Monitoring errors

These come from the monitoring service, not from the Registry API, but they appear in the same alert channels.

| Code | Name | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `MON-2001` | `SCRAPE_FAILED` | Monitoring couldn't collect metrics from one agent. Usually the agent is paused or restarting. |
| `MON-2002` | `REGISTRY_UNREACHABLE` | Monitoring failed to reach the Registry API three times in a row. It raises the `RegistryUnreachable` alert. |
</source>

<source id="D14:1" doc="D14" title="Agent owners' FAQ" section="Agent owners' FAQ > Can my agent use the biggest model?" date="2026-09-10" type="official">
## Can my agent use the biggest model?

Only on the priority tier. Standard-tier agents can use the smaller and mid-sized models. Moving to priority needs a sign-off from whoever holds your team's budget, and after that you can change the model.
</source>

<source id="D01:4" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Creating an agent" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Creating an agent

`POST /agents` creates an agent. It needs a `write` key. The body must include `agent_id`, `model`, `tier` and `owner`; `status` defaults to `active`.

```json
{"agent_id": "triage_agent", "model": "claude-haiku", "tier": "standard", "owner": "support-team"}
```

Agent ids must be unique: reusing one returns `REG-1006`. The model must be allowed on the agent's tier (see "Tiers and models"), or the request fails with `REG-1007`.
</source>

<source id="D03:3" doc="D03" title="Registry changelog" section="Registry changelog > v2.3 — 2026-03-10" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## v2.3 — 2026-03-10

- Added the `tier` field to every agent. Existing agents were set to `standard`.
- Each tier now has an allowlist of models. Assigning a model outside it returns `REG-1007`.
</source>

<source id="D07:2" doc="D07" title="Runbook: migrating agents off claude-legacy" section="Runbook: migrating agents off claude-legacy > Step 1: Check the target is allowed" date="2026-07-02" type="official">
## Step 1: Check the target is allowed

Both target models are allowed on the `standard` tier, so neither agent needs a tier change. If you'd rather move to `claude-opus`, the agent must move to the `priority` tier first, or the change fails with `REG-1007`.
</source>

<source id="D02:1" doc="D02" title="Error code reference" section="Error code reference > Request errors" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Request errors

| Code | Name | HTTP | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `REG-1005` | `AGENT_NOT_FOUND` | 404 | No agent has this `agent_id`. Ids are case-sensitive. |
| `REG-1006` | `AGENT_NAME_TAKEN` | 409 | An agent with this `agent_id` already exists, including a retired one. |
| `REG-1007` | `MODEL_NOT_ALLOWED` | 422 | The model isn't on the allowlist for the agent's tier. Change the tier first, or pick an allowed model. |
| `REG-1008` | `VALIDATION_FAILED` | 422 | The body is missing a required field or has a value of the wrong type. The message names the field. |
| `REG-1010` | `MODEL_DEPRECATED` | 422 | The model is deprecated and can't be newly assigned. Currently applies to `claude-legacy`. |
</source>

<source id="postgresql/high-availability.md:104" doc="postgresql/high-availability.md" title="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication" section="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication > Hot Standby > Handling Query Conflicts" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">
### Handling Query Conflicts

Once the delay specified by `max_standby_archive_delay` or `max_standby_streaming_delay` has been exceeded, conflicting queries will be canceled. This usually results just in a cancellation error, although in the case of replaying a `DROP DATABASE` the entire conflicting session will be terminated. Also, if the conflict is over a lock held by an idle transaction, the conflicting session is terminated (this behavior might change in the future).

Canceled queries may be retried immediately (after beginning a new transaction, of course). Since query cancellation depends on the nature of the WAL records being replayed, a query that was canceled may well succeed if it is executed again.
</source>

content.text:
Based on the runbook for agent latency investigations, here's where slowdowns usually come from:

**Most slowdowns come from tools, not the model** [D05:2].

When investigating an agent latency spike, the recommended approach is:

1. Open a few recent slow sessions and examine the time spent in each **tool call** and each **model call**.
2. You'll typically find that most spikes come from **one tool that got slow**, rather than from the model itself.
3. Write down which specific tool had the issue and when it started.

The key takeaway is that you should investigate the external tools being called by the agent, not just focus on the underlying model performance. Tools can become overloaded, have network issues, or encounter bottlenecks that cause the latency to appear as if the model itself was slow.

### Offline processing

For offline processing systems, the key metric is how long data takes to get
through the system, so page if that gets high enough to cause user impact.

<source id="prometheus-docs/practices/instrumentation.md:6" doc="prometheus-docs/practices/instrumentation.md" title="Instrumentation" section="Instrumentation > How to instrument > The three types of services > Offline processing" date="2026-09-23" type="vendor">
#### Offline processing

Knowing the last time that a system processed something is useful for detecting if it has stalled,
but it is very localised information. A better approach is to send a heartbeat
through the system: some dummy item that gets passed all the way through
and includes the timestamp when it was inserted. Each stage can export the most
recent heartbeat timestamp it has seen, letting you know how long items are
taking to propagate through the system. For systems that do not have quiet
periods where no processing occurs, an explicit heartbeat may not be needed.
</source>

Based on the company's runbooks and investigation guides, here's where slowdowns usually come from in an agent latency investigation:

**Most common source: Tools / External Services**

According to the Runbook for agent latency spike [D05:2], **"most spikes come from one tool that got slow, not from the model."** 

The typical investigation process involves:

1. **Finding the slow step** - Open recent slow sessions and examine the time spent in each tool call vs. model call. This is where most issues originate.

2. **External service issues** - Agents often depend on external tools/services like payments gateways, authentication services, or other internal APIs. Common problems include:
   - Timeout failures causing retries (as seen in incident INC-2041 with `billing_agent` [D09:2])
   - Certificate expiration leading to hung requests (auth-service timed out waiting for cert checks)
   - Rate limiting with `Retry-After` delays [D05:4]

3. **Infrastructure layer** - Registry API itself can be affected by:
   - Auth-service being slow, affecting all registry requests [D04:2]
   - Registry database unavailability [D04:2]

**Key principle from vendor documentation** - You should only page on latency at one point in a stack [prometheus-docs/practices/alerting.md]. If a lower-level component is slower but overall user latency is fine, there's no need to page separately.

So when investigating an agent latency issue, start by examining the specific tool calls rather than assuming it's the model's fault.

payments-gateway checks every request's certificate with auth-service before it will talk to a caller. | Code | Name | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `MON-2001` | `SCRAPE_FAILED` | Monitoring couldn't collect metrics from one agent. Usually the agent is paused or restarting. |
| `MON-2002` | `REGISTRY_UNREACHABLE` | Monitoring failed to reach the Registry API three times in a row. It raises the `RegistryUnreachable` alert. |

<source id="prometheus-docs/practices/alerting.md:3" doc="prometheus-docs/practices/alerting.md" title="Alerting" section="Alerting > What to alert on > Online serving systems" date="2026-09-23" type="vendor">
### Online serving systems

Typically alert on high latency and error rates as high up in the stack as possible.

Only page on latency at one point in a stack. If a lower-level component is
slower than it should be, but the overall user latency is fine, then there is
no need to page.

For error rates, page on user-visible errors. If there are errors further down
the stack that will cause such a failure, there is no need to page on them
separately. However, if some failures are not user-visible, but are otherwise
severe enough to require human involvement (for example, you are losing a lot of
money), add pages to be sent on those.
</source>

<source id="prometheus-docs/practices/instrumentation.md:1" doc="prometheus-docs/practices/instrumentation.md" title="Instrumentation" section="Instrumentation > How to instrument" date="2026-09-23" type="vendor">

service should have at least a few metrics to give you a rough idea of how it is
performing.

Instrumentation should be an integral part of your code. Instantiate the metric
classes in the same file you use them. This makes going from alert to console to code
easy when you are chasing an error.

## Overview

The Registry API stores the configuration of every agent the company runs: its name, the model it uses, its tier, its owner and its status. Agents and internal tools read it to find out how an agent is configured, and owners write to it to change that configuration. The current version is v2.6.

All endpoints live under one base URL:

```
https://registry.internal.example/v2
```

Requests and responses are JSON. Timestamps are ISO 8601 in UTC.

<source id="D14:1" doc="D14" title="Agent owners' FAQ" section="Agent owners' FAQ > Can my agent use the biggest model?" date="2026-09-10" type="official">
## Can my agent use the biggest model?

Only on the priority tier. Standard-tier agents can use the smaller and mid-sized models. Moving to priority needs a sign-off from whoever holds your team's budget, and after that you can change the model.
</source>

<source id="D01:4" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Creating an agent" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Creating an agent

`POST /agents` creates an agent. It needs a `write` key. The body must include `agent_id`, `model`, `tier` and `owner`; `status` defaults to `active`.

```json
{"agent_id": "triage_agent", "model": "claude-haiku", "tier": "standard", "owner": "support-team"}
```

Agent ids must be unique: reusing one returns `REG-1006`. The model must be allowed on the agent's tier (see "Tiers and models"), or the request fails with `REG-1007`.
</source>

Both target models are allowed on the `standard` tier, so neither agent needs a tier change. If you'd rather move to `claude-opus`, the agent must move to the `priority` tier first, or the change fails with `REG-1007`.

<source id="prometheus-docs/operating/security.md:6" doc="prometheus-docs/operating/security.md" title="Security model" section="Security model > Prometheus" date="2026-09-23" type="vendor">
## Prometheus

It is presumed that untrusted users have access to the Prometheus HTTP endpoint
and logs. They have access to all time series information contained in the
database, plus a variety of operational/debugging information.

It is also presumed that only trusted users have the ability to change the
command line, configuration file, rule files and other aspects of the runtime
environment of Prometheus and other components.

Which targets Prometheus scrapes, how often and with what other settings is
determined entirely via the configuration file. The administrator may
decide to use information from service discovery systems, which combined with
relabelling may grant some of this control to anyone who can modify data in
that service discovery system.
</source>

### Data model

Nagios is host-based. Each host can have one or more services and each service
can perform one check.

There is no notion of labels or a query language.
</source>

<source id="alertmanager/alertmanager.md:2" doc="alertmanager/alertmanager.md" title="Alertmanager" section="Alertmanager > Grouping" date="2026-09-27" type="vendor">
## Grouping

Grouping categorizes alerts of similar nature into a single notification. This
is especially useful during larger outages when many systems fail at once and
hundreds to thousands of alerts may be firing simultaneously.

**Example:** Dozens or hundreds of instances of a service are running in your
cluster when a network partition occurs. Half of your service instances
can no longer reach the database.
Alerting rules in Prometheus were configured to send an alert for each service
instance if it cannot communicate with the database. As a result hundreds of
alerts are sent to Alertmanager.
</source>
